subtopic: REPORT ON MEETING OF INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: REPORT ON MEETING OF INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a few moments of the time of the house to report on the twenty second annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development which was held last week in Rio de Janeiro. As governor of the I.M.F. and the world bank for Canada I led the Canadian delegation which this year for the first time included three other members of this house; the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for Saint-Maurice-Lafleche (Hon. Jean Chretien), and the hon. members for Essex West (Mr. Gray) and Labelle (Mr. Clermont). As I did in Rio, I should like to pay tribute again to the kindness and hospitality of our hosts in this beautiful city of Rio.
The most important item on the agenda concerning the I.M.F. was the resolution dealing with the establishment in the fund of a new facility based on special drawing rights to meet the need, as and when it arises, for a supplement to existing reserve assets. Through close consultation with our executive director on the board of the fund and through Canada's membership in the Group of Ten, Canada has actively participated in the development of the plan proposed in the resolution which was before us in Rio. Agreement on the plan was only possible by a series of compromises; consequently it was not completely in accord with Canadian views. None the less we strongly supported it, and I am pleased to report that the resolution was unanimously passed.
The resolution requests the fund's executive directors to complete the drafting of the new articles necessary to implement the proposal by March 31, 1968 at the latest. The governors will then be asked to vote on these amendments, and if they are passed the new agreement will go to the parliaments for approval and the authority to implement it.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
I stressed in Rio the importance of establishing this new facility as quickly as possible. I will be prepared to place the necessary bill before parliament very soon after approval by the governors of the detailed agreement. I hope parliament will give it full, speedy and sympathetic consideration. The setting up of this new facility will be a major step forward in strengthening the international monetary system.
Many governors including myself gave some attention to the need for national economic policies appropriate to the international and domestic circumstances of the present. The ministers and governors of the Group of Ten also took advantage of their presence in Rio to meet to discuss a problem that I know is in the minds of us all, the high level of interest rates which currently prevails throughout the world.
As for the meeting of the international bank, while the replenishment of the resources of the International Development Association was not formally on the agenda, it was the most important issue to be discussed and dominated the proceedings. The
I.D.A. is the affiliate of the world bank which extends credits on concessional or "soft" terms to developing countries that do not earn sufficient foreign exchange to service loans made on conventional terms. Past government contributions to I.D.A. which had been set at $250 million a year for three years have virtually all been committed.
I met with Mr. George Woods, president of the world bank group and with ministers of finance of countries that contribute the major part of I.D.A. resources. I told them that I consider I.D.A. to be one of the most effective and efficient means of channelling aid to developing countries. The replenishment of
I.D.A. could well be one of the most critical points in the relations between the developed and developing world. Accordingly I was most anxious to have I.D.A. replenished at a substantially higher level than in the past and indicated that, subject to parliamentary approval, Canada would be prepared to contribute its share to such a replenishment.
As a result of my conversations I am much more hopeful than before the meeting that
October 2, 1967

Meeting of International Monetary Fund such a replenishment will take place at an early date.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to have permission of the house to table the statement I made on behalf of Canada at the meeting in Rio as soon as it has been translated from English to French and from French to English.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the degree of satisfaction with which this house will have received the statement by the minister must be tempered by the fact that there is no easy road to full implementation of the first part of this international accord, and the minister has indicated some of the necessary steps that must be taken. The one point I dispute with him relates to his anticipation that he will present legislation to implement such an agreement in due course, namely sometime late in 1968 or 1969. I hope there will be a replacement by that time.
Those who have followed the deliberations of this international conference realize there are some real problems ahead. Not only is this an interim draft negotiated after some concessions; I think the minister would be the first to admit that before the governors are in a position to vote and the legislatures of the respective countries are in a position to ratify the agreement there must be more hard bargaining because of certain influences and pressures for radical change in the composition of international credit facilities.
Having said that, I should not like to minimize the contribution that has been made as a step forward in removing an area of unsettlement or unrest in respect of world credit facilities, having regard not only to the basis of exchange but a gathering of the international bank group and a decision to replenish the international development account. I am sure a great deal of the pressure and unrest in the world results from, shall we say, the agitation or the natural desire of some of the have-not countries for more extended facilities so they may develop their economies. We look forward to examining the minister's statement, which he indicated he will be tabling, and ultimately we will be examining the minister more closely during the consideration of his estimates or on some other appropriate occasion as to just what went on at this conference.

subtopic: REPORT ON MEETING OF INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure everyone who has been following the attempts that have been made to permit the world to break out of the strait-j acket it has been in for a number of years now, in fact ever since we set up the International Monetary Fund, will greet this development with considerable satisfaction. We shall, of course, be interested to know just what will be the terms upon which nations will be able to avail themselves of the special drawing rights which have been referred to by the minister.
I would hope myself that this perhaps is a first step toward a much wider and a much deeper international co-operation than is in-dictated by a purely monetary agreement. I would hope that the prophecy of the late John Maynard Keynes might eventually come true and that this sort of thing will be the first step toward some type of global administration.
Any such step, of course, will be greeted with shrieks of dismay from those who are deeply wedded to the past and its concepts of natural sovereignty. It has been obvious for a number of years that we could not go on as we have been, relying on the currencies of the United States and Great Britain and a gold supply which is really entirely beyond our control, as a means of financing world trade and world development. My only regret is that it has taken the monetary authorities of the world so many years to take even this step after the first proposals were made for developments of this sort. I have always been very pleased to note that Canada has been in the forefront in pressing for this much needed and long delayed reform.

subtopic: REPORT ON MEETING OF INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are pleased to have the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) with us again in the house after a long week of absence.
Indeed, last week we needed him when we dealt with the question of gold, of subsidies to the gold mines of northwestern Quebec, as well as the wheat subsidies. But the minister was busy in Rio de Janeiro, in Brazil, at the conference of the International Monetary Fund and the Internal Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
He has just told us that the Canadian government does not necessarily share the conclusions arrived at, and that many compromises were made to achieve unanimity- which unanimity does not satisfy the government.

October 2, 1967

Now, when, in Rio de Janeiro, discussions took place about international finance, national finance, aid to countries where it is urgently needed and also to countries where the need is not so great, I wonder if the minister, who brought there attractive suggestions for the international financial community, was not questioned about how things were going over here in Canada, in relation, specifically, to the International Monetary Fund and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
It is certainly a very good thing, Mr. Speaker, to deal with matters pertaining to international finance; still, I believe it might be more advisable, at the moment, to settle first our own national financial problems. No doubt the minister was asked about conditions prevailing in Canada, and I cannot help wondering if, at that time, he thought of calling the attention of the representatives of the various countries of the world to a statement made more than a hundred years ago by a former president of the United States, John Adams, whom I quote:
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)

All the perplexities, confusion and distress in America arise, not from defects in their constitution or confederation; not from want of honor or virtue, so much as from downright ignorance of the nature of coin, credit and circulation.

Mr. Speaker, those questions precisely were discussed at the conference of the International Monetary Fund and I agree with the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) that we must look into the minister's remarks or into the report he has just submitted.
We shall study the proposals made by that world monetary conference in order to draw some conclusions which, I hope, will open the eyes not only of a group of Canadians but of the whole people and will encourage the Canadian government to take some responsibilities in the field of finance, credit and currency in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in a young country such as Canada where the population is made up of people who have come from many countries, where there are vast distances over which people and goods must be transported, a country with a strategic location on this earth, it is natural that there will be many matters, that trouble Canadians. Canadians are serious about the unity of Canada; they are concerned about it. Canadians are worried about peace on earth, the Viet Nam situation, and the underdeveloped countries which need assistance. Parents are worried about future opportunities for their children to achieve their aims by individual effort and not by relying entirely on governments. Our people are concerned about the position of Christian principles within our society.
There are many things which concern Canadians and it is well that Canadians think about them. However, the motive of selfpreservation and self-interest-and I use the expression "self-interest" in the broad sense -is an overpowering one. Therefore I believe the one single factor with which most Canadians are concerned today is that of inflation and the increasing cost of living. Inflation steals from the poor and the prudent. I think of the elderly couple or the old age pensioner who are trying to survive on $105 a month. Out of this $105 the old age pensioner may have only $40 or $50 a month with which to provide a reasonable roof over his head. I know of many instances where such people do not have enough money toward the end of the month to satisfy their hunger.
I used the word "prudent". There are prudent people who are affected by inflation. I think of a friend of mine who retired about nine years ago. He had been a fairly senior official in a private company. Partly because of health reasons he retired at a somewhat early age, although he was not required to do so. He had given his family a reasonable home life. He had sent his children through school. He had never looked to any government for a handout. He had saved money and he had bought bonds. With his savings he bought a house. From the income on an annuity which he had bought and from the interest on his bonds he thought at the time he retired that he would be able to maintain a reasonable standard of living. Today he finds that the value of his annuity and the income from his bonds are not sufficient to
Discussion on Housing maintain him at a reasonable standard. He is now forced to sell some of his bonds. He figured he would try to live on some of his capital until he became eligible for old age security, but he finds that he is receiving only about 80 per cent on the dollar for the bonds he is selling.
I think of the hundreds and thousands of retired civil servants, many of whom have made representations to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the government. They have indicated that in many instances the pensions they received at the time of retirement will now buy only 60 per cent of what they would have bought at the time they were retired. Truly inflation and the increasing cost of living do steal from the poor and the prudent.
But there is one aspect of Canadian life on which inflation has a devastating effect and that is housing. Housing is an essential element for the social well-being of the citizens of the country. Last Monday, on behalf of our party, I moved the adjournment of the house to consider a matter of urgent national importance, namely, the housing crisis. Realizing that the question would be raised by us again and that the motion might well be granted at a later date, the government therefore agreed to bring up the estimates of the Department of Labour last Thursday so that we could discuss the crisis.
I wish to make it clear that I do not use the word "crisis" in the sense that this is a problem which has arisen just now; it is a problem which has been with us for a long time. Repeatedly we have brought it to the attention of the government. For example, on May 16, 1966, a year and half ago, the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) moved the following amendment to a supply motion:
The policies of the government in imposing tight money and denying builders and prospective home owners needed mortgage funds, constitute a negative approach to the problems facing our economy and are seriously impeding the development of the nation.
Let me describe briefly what the current situation is with regard to housing. We have brought it to the attention of the government before but it may need repeating in a brief manner. At page 193 of the fourth annual review of the Economic Council of Canada we find the following:
Nevertheless it appears that perhaps as many as one million Canadians are housed in substandard dwellings of this description.

October 2, 1967
Discussion on Housing
The reference is to a backlog in housing requirements. Roughly one million people were in need of housing this year as of the date of this report. I should like to quote from page 129 of the report of the special committee of the Senate on aging:
-300,000 elderly family and non-family households in 1961-were experiencing difficulties in their housing situation.
As a matter of fact, Mr. R. Adamson, C.M.H.C. economist, estimated when he appeared before the Senate committee on aging that at least 400,000 elderly persons as of that date were in need of housing assistance because of the backlog in the housing situation. What is being done to solve this backlog in housing requirements? I should like to quote from page 133 of the same report of the Economic Council of Canada:
We estimate that by the end of the 1960's housing starts and completions in Canada will need to rise to annual levels of at least 200,000 units to fully meet the nation's requirements at that time.
At another point it states that in the last four years of the 1960's an average of 194,000 housing starts will be required to meet the current requiremetns. Just speaking of one place, the city of Victoria and its environs, the capital regional planning board of British Columbia, at the time I was chairman, made a survey of housing requirements for elderly people in the greater Victoria area and arrived at the conclusion that at least 1,000 people in that area alone were in urgent need of housing accommodation. That is the present situation in respect of housing.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
What is being done to meet, first of all, the current requirements and, second, to catch up on the backlog of shortages? In 1966 there were 134,000 housing starts in Canada. The minister indicated last week that this year there will be in the order of 150,000 housing starts.
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member would not want to allow a misstatement to go by unchallenged. The figure I mentioned last Thursday was 150,000, not 130,000.

Perhaps the minister
misunderstood me. I did say that he estimated there will be 150,000 starts this year. In any event, in those two years alone, over and above the one million houses the Economic Council of Canada suggests are required there has been a shortage of requirement in the neighbourhood of 70,000 to 90,000 houses.

Therefore we are falling farther and farther behind.
Having recognized the situation as it is, let us consider the effect of this critical situation on Canadians. Let me refer first of all to page 136 of the report of the Economic Council of Canada. It enumerates certain effects which result from the housing situation in Canada including:
-shortages of suitable housing in many of the larger urban areas of the country, with adverse social consequences and inhibiting effects on labour mobility;
-widespread and significant increases in rents and house prices, which have been reflected in the cost of living and in upward pressures on wages

In the 12 months ended August, 1967, the consumer price index on housing went up from 145 to 152.2, an increase of 7.2 in one year alone. It is common knowledge that the shortage of housing in itself has tremendously increased the cost of houses which have been built. It is obvious that when there are more purchasers than there are houses the price goes up.
The third effect as reported at page 136 of the council's report is:
-the sharp drop-off in the utilization of productive capacity in the apartment building sector of the construction industry, with disruptive effects on efficiencies and on the longer-term retention of specialized and skilled labour.
Let me emphasize again the effect on apartment buildings. The minister indicated, and generally authorities agree, that the most efficient form of housing is the multiple type, not necessarily apartment blocks because it could include row houses. This does not mean that people who want to own their own houses should not be allowed to do so, but from the point of view of the provision of houses and the cost of land and services, apartment or multiple housing units are more efficient. The Economic Council points out that the existing situation has had a severe effect on this particular phase of the house construction industry.
Let me refer to a few words of a contractor in my area who has written to the minister to indicate the effect of this housing policy on contractors. First of all he says it prevents builders from building speculative housing which could be used to level out builders' production. Second, it makes it impossible for builders to engage in any kind of realistic planning or buying because builders cannot get volume prices and price discounts on material and subcontracts when neither they nor their suppliers know how many housing
October 2. 1967

starts they will have in the next few weeks, let alone in the next few months.
This man also suggests that builders cannot afford to develop land when the lack of mortgage money makes land unusable for months, leaving capital tied up. He suggests that banks are not interested in developing land of that sort. Therefore builders must wait for mortgage funds to be released and then scramble for whatever lands are available at a premium price which must be passed on to the consumer.
I am trying to point out the effect of the housing situation on Canadians. Let me quote from page 25 of the report of the Economic Council of Canada:
Many potential home-owner borrowers, for example, may be deterred by virtue of the fact that a higher mortgage interest rate finds significant reflection in the size of the monthly mortgage payment, particularly given the long-term nature of most of the loans now made.
Last week we attempted to point out the seriousness of the existing housing situation. Last Thursday we listened with a great deal of interest and anticipation to replies and answers from members on the government side. It was my impression that the general reaction of the government was, first of all, that this is not a serious situation and, second, that if it is serious there is nothing it can do about it. For example, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) seems to be more concerned about the actual number of housing starts that should be made according to the report than the fact we are falling farther and farther behind. He has consoled himself with the fact that this year housing starts are 15 per cent above the level of 1966. What he did not say was that in 1966 there were
32.000	fewer starts than in 1965. Surely the number of starts should not be anything else but greater. The minister did not mention that the number of housing starts in 1966 was less than in 1958 when there were 164,000. The number of starts last year was less than in 1955 when there were 138,000.
The minister seems to be unconcerned about the fact that the Economic Council has pointed out that 140,000 houses are required per annum for new family formations and nonfamily requirements and that in addition
50.000	are required for replacement. Apparently this is not important. To indicate the attitude of the government let me refer to page 2596 of Hansard for September 28, 1967.
Discussion on Housing The minister interjected with this question to the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott):
Does he know that from among those who have borrowed in excess of $500 million this year more than half the borrowers have incomes between $4,000 and $7,000 a year?
That question clearly implied that if that amount of money was borrowed by people earning between $4,000 and $7,000 per year there should be no difficulty in respect of those people who are earning less than $8,000 per year. What the minister fails to bring to the attention of the house is that according to the Canadian housing statistics for 1966 the average cost of a house to those people whose income was less than $4,000 was $12,560. The down payment required from the people in that group was $7,000. The minister knows the C.M.H.C. requirement that the payment to retire the debt and cover the taxes must not exceed 27 per cent of one's gross income. So the people in the low income group to whom the minister referred had to put up a great deal of cash in order to reduce their mortgages.

These people often had to borrow the money, without C.M.H.C.'s knowledge, in order to make the down payment. They borrow the money or sell a little home they have and they put down a large sum of money in order to meet the requirements of C.M.H.C. I am trying to point up the attitude of the government in this respect.
The hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mac-kasey) spent a great deal of time the other day reading to the house excerpts from various newspapers indicating in effect that many houses are available and there is no problem at all. I think the hon. member spent ten minutes trying to convince us that there was no problem at all. In view of that attitude of the government we believe we should continue to bring to its attention the serious situation that exists.
Last Thursday the Minister of Labour said to us in effect: What does the Economic Council of Canada advise us to do? Do they prescribe any solutions for tiiis serious problem?
This brings me to the next point I wish to make. First of all, we should try to recognize what were the factors that caused the present situation, what were the conditions that led to it. How can any government find a solution to a problem unless it first recognizes the causes of the problem? I now wish to deal with the causes that led to this crisis in

Discussion on Housing housing. I quote from page 261 of the fourth annual review of the Economic Council of Canada:
Thus, the accelerated increase in government spending in 1966 and 1967 is outpacing the growth of government revenues at existing tax levels.
Now we are getting to the crux of the matter and the cause of the situation in which we find ourselves with respect to housing. I must point out that the excerpt I have just read from the fourth annual review of the Economic Council refers to government spending and includes all levels of government. Let us never say that the whole fault lies with the federal government. But I submit that according to the figures quoted in the report of the Economic Council of Canada the increase in spending by this government has been a major factor in arriving at the situation where it is not possible to obtain private money with which to finance housing mortgages.
On page 27 of the fourth annual review of the Economic Council of Canada the increases in expenditures of all governments are set out. For example, in the case of goods and services federal government expenditures in 1966 increased by 18.8 per cent over 1965. If we exclude defence, the increase in expenditures in 1966 over 1965 was 27.1 per cent. When the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith) spoke in the budget debate on June 6 last he indicated that the increase in federal government expenditures in 1967 over 1966 would be another 20 per cent. We are trying to find out what are the factors which led to the situation we face today.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, could I ask the hon. gentleman a question?

Mr. Speaker, I would prefer to answer questions at the end of my speech. We are trying to put our finger on the cause of this serious situation. The government has taken the attitude that there is a shortage of money and this is the reason they have had to raise the interest rate on C.M.H.C. loans to a maximum of 8J per cent. I agree with the minister that this does not mean the interest rate will be 8i per cent. That is the maximum. It may well be that it will not go up to 8J per cent.
The government says there is a shortage of money and they ask: What else could we do? The question is, Mr. Speaker, why is there this shortage of money? I wish to quote rather extensively from the speech of the hon. member for Perth in the budget debate of June 6 because the hon. member put his
[Mr. Chatterton.l
finger on the cause of this situation in which money cannot be obtained at a reasonable rate for housing mortgages. I quote from page 1192 of Hansard of June 6 last:
The other evening the minister casually brushed over the effect on the money markets, interest rates, international affairs and domestic prices-
And so on. I quote further from the hon. member's speech as reported on the same page of Hansard:
All the signs point to the government having to move into the money market in a very big way.
I listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) announce just a few minutes ago that this is a trend right across the world. I realize there is concern in Europe and many other western countries particularly because the United States is using the interest rate to ease the economy. I believe that the action of this government has greatly aggravated the situation which exists in Canada, though it is subject to influence from other parts of the world. The action of the government has contributed directly to the position in which we find ourselves today, where money at a reasonable rate cannot be obtained to finance such an essential article as housing. I quote again from the speech of the future minister, now the hon. member for Perth, at page 1193 of Hansard. I said "future minister", and I mean in the not too distant future.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext: You must mean that he is turning ecclesiastical.

As reported at page 1193 of Hansard, the hon. member for Perth said:
As the minister noted, prices are now 7.3 per cent above what they were two years ago. It is obvious, sir, that the grocery dollar is getting smaller and smaller. At the same time that prices are rising the government must attempt to raise funds of its own in competition with private business and with individuals so in effect the price of borrowing money rises too.
The hon. member then said, as reported on the same page:
It means interest rates will tend to stay high.
Further, the hon. member said, as reported at page 1193 of Hansard:
Sir my concern with the financial gyrations of this government is that it has a total disregard for the expenditure of the peoples' money.
We are beginning to put our finger upon what has caused or aggravated the housing shortage in this country. I shall now read a few of the excerpts which the hon. member in his speech read from the Globe and Mail
October 2, 1967

of June 5. This appears at page 1195 of Hansard for June 6:
In the past several years the public has acquired a good deal of experience in the methods of frenzied financiers and it therefore should have no great difficulty in recognizing the glibness of Finance Minister Sharp for what it is.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
In his budget speech, which is the equivalent of the annual report to shareholders from the president of a financial institution, the finance minister put up a bold front, yet he was unable to conceal the one important fact, that the nation's financial operations are out of control.
Last Thursday members of all the opposition parties tended to blame only the Minister of Labour. I think he should carry a certain measure of blame for the situation in which we find ourselves today but I submit the basic cause leading to this problem does not lie with the Minister of Labour except in so far as he is a member of the government. It can be directly ascribed to the policies of this government as indicated by the Minister of Finance. It is he who has mainly contributed to the situation we face today.
I could continue quoting along the same lines for another half hour. I am trying to find explanations for the basic causes which have led to this situation. First of all I wish to quote from pages 108 and 109 of the report of the Economic Council of Canada. Reference is made here to the surplus and deficit positions on a national accounts basis. The expert reads as follows:
The major factor in this development in 1966 was an extraordinary rise in government purchases of goods and services, of 16 per cent, or $1.6 billion, the largest percentage increase since the Korean defence build-up.
A very significant comment is made on page 24 of the fourth annual review of the Economic Council of Canada regarding the shortage of housing. It reads as follows:
It is important to note that this situation has not developed as a result of any conscious choice, based on an ordering of the national priorities.
What is meant there is that the government has been drafted into this position because of a lack of a firm stand and because of a lack of a recognition of priorities.
Now let me quote a very eminent journalist and a great columnist, Mr. Bruce Hutchison, from the Ottawa Journal of September 25. The article reads partly as follows:
The Pearson government is trying desperately to extricate itself from a double blunder of economics and politics.
Farther on he wrote the following:
The moment of financial truth came in the last month when the government suddenly found that
Discussion on Housing it could not sell its bonds without paying exorbitant interest rates which have automatically raised those of all borrowers, public and private.
Mr. Hutchison, who I think is a greater authority on this subject than I am, went on to say:
Finally it found its fiscal policies under unprecedented attack by the impartial Economic Council-
Up to now the government, misjudging the economic climate has fed inflation with its deficits.
I do not think there is any doubt in anybody's mind that inflation is a factor which has contributed more than anything else to the position which we have a right to take today in the housing crisis.
Now I wish to quote the following from the Financial Post of September 2 of this year:
Ottawa can only blame itself for its present boxed-in position. If its increases in spending had been less exuberant across the board in the past few years, it would now be able to borrow more easily to finance its long-established housing program.
Farther on the same editorial, headed "Why .Housing Gets Hit", reads as follows:
If our political leaders in their beneficence wish to improve the outlook for housing in a more permanent way they must design and time their total spending in a way that encourages, not discourages, private investment in housing.
I think we are beginning to make our case. We recognize there is a shortage of money and tremendous competition in the capital market. We are trying to find out reasons for that situation, and I maintain it was the action of this government which has greatly contributed to that difficult position. I feel sorry for the Minister of Labour. I know he would like to go to the government and say: Please give me another $300 million so I can make direct loans available rather than have to raise the interest rate. I am sure he would love to be in a position where the Minister of Finance would agree to giving him $300 million more.
I recognize that the government has spent $900 million this year, but why did it have to do so? It is because the action of the government has made it impossible for private lenders to have money available to lend for housing. This is why the government has had to spend money on housing. I commend the government for having spent that much in difficult times, but why did it have to do it? Next year we will be in a worse position. As the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) told us on Thursday, next year we will not be able to get nearly as much. Therefore the

Ociober 2, 1967
Discussion on Housing government has to rely on a fantastically high interest rate to induce private investors to put their money into housing. I appreciate the position of the Minister of Labour and I acknowledge it is not of his making. I see the minister is smiling.
Mr. Connelly, the president of the National House Builders Association, had the following to say as reported in the association's news release of August 24, 1967:
Mr. Connelly said that his association shared the government's concern for deficit financing and he pointed out that heavy government borrowings at all levels to maintain many non-essential programs had cut into the supply of mortgage money. He agreed with the hope of the government that by reducing its demands on the capital market it will cause interest rates to fall and that more private money will then be attracted into mortgages.
There is not much hope of that now; they may go up to 8.25 per cent. I wish to quote now from the Telegram of September 29 in which the following comment is made:
Is Ottawa so blind to the growing inflation in this country, brought on in part by unwise government spending, not to know that even upper income families cannot afford new homes?
Are the government's expenditures in relation to its revenues in such desperate straits that it must sweeten the prospects of private capital buying up N.H.A. mortgages at the expense of the would-be home owner?
There is no doubt that the people who will suffer most from the present situation and from the present action of the government, which was in effect necessary because of the past actions of the government, are the people who can afford it least, namely, people earning less than $8,000 a year.
The Minister of Labour asked us on Thursday what the solution to the problem is. He said that the Economic Council of Canada did not put forward any constructive proposals. As I have said before, the first step is for the government to recognize the causative factors which led to the situation. Unless it recognizes and accepts them, how can it remove the causes?
I hope I have achieved something by impressing on the government that it was their actions that brought about the situation where mortgage money cannot be obtained for housing at a reasonable rate. The government should realize what is required in a practical way to achieve the objectives outlined by the Economic Council of Canada. On page 112 of its report the Economic Council wrote the following:
The increase in the housing stock, on the other hand, has not kept pace with the rise in new family and household formation in the recent period. Vacancy rates have been sharply reduced,

and the price of housing and rental accommodation has risen sharply. Over the period 1963-66, the average rate of growth in the physical volume of housing expenditures amounted to only 3.2 per cent per year.
This is what will be required from now on and the government should pay special attention to it. The report continues:
To meet the demand for housing which our projections of new family and household formation imply, an average of some 190,000 new housing units per year are required between the years 1966 and 1970. This would mean an average annual rate of growth in the real physical volume of housing expenditures of about 8.4 per cent per year to 1970, or well over twice the average rate for the 1983-66 period.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the government must be aware that this sum of money will be required from now on to meet the minimum objectives which have been set by the Economic Council. Unless they realize this, how can they take action to achieve those objectives?
On the negative side, on page 265 of the report of the Economic Council of Canada there is the following statement:
The use of housing as an economic regulator should not be continued to such an extent in the future.
This is also something the government must keep in mind. There must be an even flow of funds for housing so that the housing industry can operate in an efficient and effective manner in order to meet the needs for housing in Canada before too many years pass. On page 264 of the report of the Economic Council it is stated:
Of all the major sectors of the economy, none will have to grow more rapidly than housing- at least to 1970.
It is set forth on page 261 that there is a need-
-for consistent and comprehensive determination of objectives and priorities:-
Let us recognize, Mr. Speaker, what is important. Is housing important? If so, let us assign to it a certain priority, and let the government arrange its fiscal affairs in such manner that the objectives set by that priority can be achieved. The report goes on to say there is also a need-
-for continuing evaluation of the impact and effectiveness of the growing range and diversity of government programs in relation to their cost; and for increased co-ordination between governments in relation to these matters.
Then at page 262 the report continues:
Similarly, careful attention should be given to the possible ways in which rising government
October 2, 1967

spending could impinge, with adverse effects on the whole economy, on needed growth in housing, exports, and business investment.
If the government does nothing else but take heed of that advice by the Economic Council of Canada and recognizes that it should not repeat the errors of the past which caused this situation, then we have gone a long way toward finding a solution to these problems. But it is a prerequisite to any solution, Mr. Speaker, to recognize the causes of the situation and to take the advice of the Economic Council not to repeat the same actions which would lead to the same problems.
Other specific suggestions could also be made. I agree with the minister when he states what is the first obligation of the government. As reported at page 2577 of Hansard the Minister of Labour said:
As I have just indicated, the government intends to devote a larger proportion of its resources to the social needs of the lower income groups and to the trouble spots resulting from the fantastic urban growth that has taken place, in order to provide improved living conditions in urban areas.
I agree that it is the prime responsibility of the government to provide housing for those in greatest need, and I concede that there have been substantial improvements under the National Housing Act in the provision of housing to accommodate people in the low income brackets. But judging from the performance last year and this year, the fact of the matter is that the measures provided under the National Housing Act have not been effective.
For example, during the whole of 1966 only 5,676 housing units were provided under the National Housing Act. We must keep in mind that the Senate report on aging indicated that there is now an immediate requirement for
300,000	such units. In addition to the 5,676 units provided by the public housing authority, another 1,300 units were provided by way of the acquisition and renovation of existing property. In the first six months of 1967 a grand total of 1,170 housing units were provided for those in greatest need in the very low income brackets.
I realize that the minister has been criticized for being absent from the house, but I commend him for having travelled around the country trying to convince provinces and municipalities that these provisions of the act can help them solve their problems. I admit that the provinces and municipalities have been reluctant to accept this proposition, but both the minister and the provinces have
Discussion on Housing made some progress in this field. For example, eight of the provinces have now established agencies to co-ordinate these provisions so that advantage may be taken of them. Nevertheless I still submit to the minister that the provisions themselves require substantial improvement.
One of the biggest difficulties

I have experienced this situation myself-is that the municipalities have to find the finances required to purchase such land and then to service it. Therefore I urge the minister to consider amending the terms of the National Housing Act by going beyond the provision of assistance for sewers and assisting the municipalities in meeting their public housing needs in other ways. I think that this is one of the fields that the municipalities are the most reluctant to enter.

If the hon. member will permit me a question, does he not know that under the act at the present time there is provision for assisting municipalities and provinces in the acquisition of land, that there are provisions for land assembly to meet future needs?

Yes, I agree. This is by agreement with the provinces. But the fact of the matter is that the municipalities still find it difficult to provide services. I point out that in some fields the federal government offers no assistance. Also it is only through federal-provincial agreement that assistance is provided in the acquisition of land.
Another aspect which could be improved substantially is that of limited dividend housing. These operations were largely at a standstill last year and only 300 units have been provided this year. Although this field is open to private capital, I think changes should be made in the provisions to ensure that private capital is given the chance to enter that field.
I do not want to take much more time, Mr. Speaker, but I point out that many excellent suggestions are made in the last chapter of the fourth annual review of the Economic Council of Canada under the heading "Policy Implications". I was glad to see that when the minister spoke last Thursday he recognized that there would have to be a thorough, comprehensive study made of the whole question of urbanization. I know this question was mentioned in the throne speech last May, but that was in May, Mr. Speaker. The minister has used the excuse that there are three provincial elections coming up and that we will have to wait until these are over, but I would ask him why he did not conduct this

October 2, 1967
Discussion on Housing study before. I am sure it is not the personal fault of the minister, but there does seem to be some confusion on the part of the government about what to do first. To my mind an objective, comprehensive study is certainly essential.
The provision of money for housing is not the only problem, as the minister knows. We also have to find the land, and there is the question of transportation to be considered. The whole thing is tied up with education and air pollution and the problem is a broad one. But I must say that unless a reasonable amount of funds is made available to provide housing we will not begin to find a solution. This is an urgent problem for which the government must find a fairly reasonable answer in the very near future.
I am going to move now to a motion which will give those members, particularly those on the other side of the house, who feel that the government by its actions has not contributed in any way to meeting this difficulty an opportunity to indicate their disapproval. It will also give those who feel that the government's policies have been demonstrated to be completely satisfactory and adequate a chance to vote against my motion. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Keays):
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"This House asserts that the government by Its failure to assign priorities to essential programs and to co-ordinate fiscal policy to ensure the carrying out of such programs, has directly contributed to the difficulty of providing adequate housing at reasonable cost; that its recent action with respect to the interest rate has worsened the position of Canadians in the middle and low income brackets;
And this House regrets the failure of the government to recognize the housing shortage as a major crisis requiring immediate and co-ordinated steps for its solution as clearly indicated by the recent report of the Economic Council of Canada."

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The
question is on the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I welcome the amendment moved by the speaker for the official opposition because it clearly expresses our party's objectives vis-a-vis the attitude of the present government to housing needs. I particularly refer to the last part of the amendment which says that the government has failed to recognize at this time the urgency of the housing crisis. I believe that the amendment clearly
[Mr. Chatterton.l
expresses the feelings not only of the official opposition and of our party but also of the Canadian people at this time. I intend to devote my time to expressing as well as I can what we feel about the utter bankruptcy of the government's policy in the face of the urgent housing situation.
There is little need for me to cite the report of the Economic Council as the previous speaker did that most carefully. To my mind the one thing this government lacks to deal with the housing crisis is the will to deal with it. I do not believe that money, materials or manpower are the essential ingredients which are lacking. The most necessary ingredient that is lacking is the will by this government to give housing the top priority that it ought to have.
Some hon. members may not think that this is a sophisticated way to talk of housing. I do not aim to be sophisticated. I aim to come before this house and to express the needs of my constituency, province and country as ably as I can. In the minds and lives of thousands across this country the need for housing has become the top priority at this time. In spite of the copious warnings in different parts of the Economic Council's report the government has no notion at all of dealing with housing as a matter of top priority.
The report was published approximately a week before we met here on September 25. In the report of the Economic Council are listed five goals of government policy. They are the five most important goals within the domestic field. At the top of the list is supplying adequate housing for the people of this country. No. 2 is educating the growing population; No. 3 is providing employment; No. 4 is maintaining price stability and No. 5 is solving urban problems.
Those of us who spent the summer in our constituencies, particularly if we live in urban constituencies, came to believe from our experience with our constituencies and constituents that housing would be the top to face parliament this fall. The government was warned about this. The Economic Council made it clear that housing should be the top priority in government policy this fall.
We returned to this House on September 25 and what did we find? First, housing was not mentioned at all on the order paper. Where was that question of urgent and top priority in the government's immediate legislative
October 2, 1967

program? Second, we found that the government resisted a discussion of the matter in the house. No provision had been made for discussion. When some hon. members pointed out that this was a matter of grave and urgent concern the government resisted discussing it. Ultimately, under great pressure a period for the discussion of this question was provided.
Third, we discovered that the entire matter of housing had been left for a federal-provincial conference which will be held some time this winter. I know that the provincial elections raise difficulties for housing conferences. Nevertheless, if a matter is of top urgency I maintain that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) ought not to announce that he will meet with the provincial premiers at some future time in the winter to discuss the field of housing. That is not how one handles the No. 1 problem of the country.
Fourth, we heard the announcement two days after parliament reconvened that the interest rate on N.H.A. loans had been raised from 7i per cent to 8J per cent.
Shame.

Again, such a measure was flying directly in the face of the advice given by the Economic Council. That body had warned over and over again that housing should not be considered a regulator of the economy and that the money tap should not be turned on and off at will. The Economic Council warned that the housing sector ought to be protected in so far as possible from the full effects of monetary policy and should not have to suffer the full effects of any monetary restraints. Actually when action was taken it did not come in the form of restraints. Instead a go-ahead signal was given to banks and other private lending institutions to add an additional full percentage point to their interest rates.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
There were monetary restraints, but they were not on the banks and the lending institutions. A tight money policy was firmly clamped on the ordinary people of this country who can no longer afford to buy homes at the present interest rate.
At present, in order to qualify for an N.H.A. loan at 8J per cent one has to have a minimum income of $8,000, and in order to carry a maximum $18,000 mortgage for a 25-year term it will cost $140.28 per month, not counting taxes. Thanks to this new government policy only well-to-do people can
Discussion on Housing
now afford to buy houses in Canada. It is the only policy the government has announced to date, and it makes it doubly certain that henceforth only well-to-do people can buy homes in this country. Certainly this was not what the ordinary people were anticipating.
In addition to the high interest rate the profit margin is a big factor in housing for people all across Canada. I have here the September bulletin of the Vancouver housing association, published before the new interest rate was announced. It points out that the shortage of mortgage money is not the only problem facing the home buyer. It also points out that a comparison of 6,000 new house sales in metropolitan Toronto during the first six months of 1965 and 1967 respectively showed that prices had risen by 26 per cent to 48 per cent, depending on areas, during the last two years. The average price of new houses sold this year was very close to $30,000. It adds:
In the Vancouver area the house cost index prepared for the Society of Residential Appraisers rose by less than 3 per cent between 1966 and 1967, but the price of new houses has risen during the same period by something nearer to 20 per cent, owing to the higher profit margins now obtainable.
What has the government done to control those higher profit margins? Has it done anything to show it would be desirable to control them?
I would like now to deal mainly with those income groups which are suffering tremendously because of the government's lack of recognition of the urgency of the situation. Had I the time, Mr. Speaker, I could tell you about many individual cases in my own riding and in other parts of Vancouver, with which I came in contact this summer. I can think of a woman with two children who travelled throughout that city using rental advertisements in the paprs in seeking a home. She had money to pay a good rental for a house but she could not find one where children were allowed. She had a car to travel around in but nowhere to live except in her sister's already too cramped quarters.
I can think of a woman in my own constituency, an amputation case, confined part time to a wheel chair and the rest of the time on crutches. She had to leave her basement suite, and a pitiful place it was, at the end of September. But she had literally no place to go. She went to all the agencies in Vancouver. First she went to the Vancouver housing authority which deals with low rental subsidized housing. Then she went to all

October 2, 1967
Discussion on Housing the other various housing associations, including the Vancouver housing association and the registry which was set up for a few days by the mayor's office but which I believe has since been closed.
I am informed that this registry office received some 11 or 12 calls over a period of five or six days offering accommodation, but one of the offers was at a rental of $225 per month. Finally she ended up where she began, with the Vancouver housing authority. There she was told, "We are very sorry. There are 1,700 people waiting for low rent publicly subsidized housing. Some 900 of them are single people like yourself, some of them disabled, but nothing short of death can make a vacancy available. Only death can bring about a vacancy for you or for anyone else in your position."
This is a terrible situation. I do not want to load all the blame upon the minister or the government. These sins go away back. This is a matter of arrears piled on arrears, piled on arrears, and we are sinking deeper and deeper into the quagmire of homelessness in which thousands of people across the country are caught. Something must be done because the problem is urgent.
Earlier this year the Vancouver city council finally took its courage in its hands. In May it produced five projects to provide housing for people with low incomes.

Does the hon. member not know that it was the Minister of Labour himself, who suggested such action to the city of Vancouver and that at a meeting in Vancouver he pleaded with the Vancouver council to act and said that the federal funds needed were already available?

know the minister is interested in this matter personally. I know he has gone to Vancouver and done his best to get various union organizations, co-operative organizations, societies of various kinds, probably veterans' organizations although these have already been involved, and other groups, to take their surplus funds and put them into housing.
The question I asked was, does the hon. member not know that I pleaded with the representatives of the city council of Vancouver to show more initiative.

Yes, I do know that and I appreciate it. However, this is what happened. In May the Vancouver

city council went to the provincial government in Victoria with five projects for housing. In August it took five more projects to Victoria. But since then those project plans have been sitting on the desk of the provincial minister in Victoria, and according to what the provincial government says none of them will be proceeded with until such time as an exhaustive cost probe has been completed by the provincial government.
The Vancouver city council, a creature of the province, having been turned down by its parent, decided to approach Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. It begged the corporation to help acquire land for these projects. What was the corporation's answer? Undoubtedly it did what it had to do under the rules. It simply said it could not help in negotiations for the purchase of land at the price to which land had risen.
e (4:30 p.m.)
As a result on September 25, the day parliament reopened, the Vancouver city planner recommended to the council that three of the ten projects be abandoned and that five others be postponed. These eight projects would have provided 484 housing units. The two remaining ones, smaller in size and designed for elderly people, should be proceeded with, according to the city officials. So out of the ten housing projects which the minister urged them to go ahead with, three are to be abandoned, five postponed and only two small ones proceeded with on the recommendation of the city planner. The reason given for this was the high cost of sites which was four times higher than previously and the fact that Victoria could not or would not approve these shared cost projects until their own cost probe was finished. C.M.H.C. in the past had refused to authorize negotiations to buy these sites. I do not know what will transpire in the period of those two weeks but I imagine that C.M.H.C., with its present instructions and policy, cannot do anything more than has been done in the past.
The problem of land assembly and land cost must be dealt with. I know that it comes under provincial jurisdiction so I do not need to be told this. But here we have a situation in respect of which the city does not have the resources to act. The provincial government apparently will not act at the present time and the federal government takes the attitude

If this is an emergency issue I think Ottawa will have to draft a workable over-all plan in respect of all kinds of housing -public, private, separate domiciles, row housing, garden apartments, high rise, and low rental subsidized housing. I know about the seminars the minister has held throughout the country. I know that within the Lmit of these he has been doing the best he can. That, however, is not what I mean. right; you may put the war in a holy category if you like but I do not. Although there had been a depression and there was no money available for anything, when war broke out we cut the red tape. We will not achieve this by sitting here in Ottawa and saying that they must come here and see us about it.
The problem of housing is the war on poverty. The Privy Council issued a pamphlet before the summer which advises us of the priorities that Canadians have. These are partly because we have not had our sights raised for us by government policy and example. We are told that in an average year Canadians spend $500 million on travel abroad, $1 billion on alcohol, $400 million at the racetracks, $200 million on candy and $30 million on dog and cat food. What we spend on public housing is less than what we spend on dog and cat food.
I am not blaming the minister, but I am saying that the present housing policy is completely ineffective. It is just like holding out a straw to a drowning man. If you say to me, "Well, where is your detailed housing policy", I say to you it is up there in the gallery and in the offices around Ottawa. It is not the ability to set up a housing policy which is lacking at this time, nor is there a lack of

Discussion on Housing brains to do it. We have the ability and the brains in offices throughout Ottawa and in the provinces and cities of this country. It is the will to build homes for the people which is lacking.
Before you say that it will cost too much, let me remind you that the lives of thousands of Canadians across this country have been blighted because of the failure to build decent modern houses. If we take one of the most depressed groups, the Indian people, they have never had a chance because of the hovels and the misery in which they live. They live in hovels in which self-respecting people would not want to keep their animals. Many of them are living in conditions of that kind.
I could take you through areas in my riding where, although we have one fairly decent low-cost subsidized housing project, there are no facilities whatsoever, or at least there were none prior to this summer, for recreation or programs of development of any kind for the people who live there. After a great deal of hard work the Vancouver housing authority finally got the money to put up a fence around two tot lots in order to keep the pre-school children from being injured by traffic on the adjacent streets. Some people did not like the particular locations of these tot lots and felt they could find available land in better areas. One of the Vancouver housing authority officials suggested to me that this was probably right but said, "For goodness sake, don't mention it to Ottawa because we would be required to instal new toilets at such locations and it would take at least two years of negotiation with Ottawa before we could obtain the money for the new toilets." I just mention that as an example of the fact that we are not dealing with these things as we should.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
We are supposed to be engaged in a war on poverty and one might ask where we might obtain the money to do the things required. Let me remind hon. members that almost all of the corporation tax revenue received by the federal government is being spent in two areas of federal responsibility, defence and borrowing. It is my feeling that we could cut down a great deal on our defence expenditure, although I realize not everyone will agree with me in this regard. Nevertheless, it is a fact that the federal government is spending about 40 per cent of its total revenue for defence and interest on borrowing.
Surely it is more important for the country to have a sound and satisfied population than

to spend a great deal of money on military hardware for defence. We should first consider provision of modern and comfortable homes. I am sure that by doing so we would be spending our money more effectively than by spending it on defence. In this nuclear age it is far more important to have a sound, healthy and happy population than a huge defence system.
Those are the comments I wanted to make this afternoon, and if I have not made them in a satisfactory manner it is because I have not got the capacity to do better. I feel very strongly that I have voiced the opinion of the people in my riding and the whole Vancouver area, particularly so far as urgency is concerned. Hundreds of people in my area will never have the opportunity of becoming home owners because there is no earthly way they can get a down payment. They do not want low rental public housing, although there are thousands of people who require this type of accommodation. I urge the government to consider seriously its new role as we enter the second century of confederation. If we want to keep Canada as one nation we will have to provide a high standard of living, adequate housing and training, and opportunities for all. This government has not yet been prepared to provide leadership in this regard. I am sure the people will continue to demand these things until their needs are satisfied.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on this motion that the house go into committee of supply-I was going to say to make some criticism-to make what I would call mainly remarks. We certainly do not have to prove to the minister the housing needs in Canada; he is as convinced as we are about that. We do not have to convince him further. However, we are more inclined to pity him instead of criticizing him severely. We pity this team caught in a strait jacket because of our fiscal system which imposes its will on Canada as a whole and makes puppets out of our ministers.
Each time I study some characteristics of our fiscal system, I feel the presence of a hidden power that it is impossible for us to detex-mine for the very good reason that it hides behind legislation. That despicable power often forces the government to do things it would rather not to do and not to do things that it would very much like to do.

Some members of this house travel around the country saying: Look at what we have done. Then at the end of the year, the government will put on our statute books all the legislation it has passed. If only that head of a family was not forced to go through a contractor to get a loan from Central Mortgage and Housing

Mr. Speaker, this legislation is only a smoke screen. Not even 10 per cent of the low-income people could qualify under the provisions of that legislation. But does the head of a family have to struggle over the payment of a house when the main concern of the government is to pass legislation to protect and assist the people, to lay down conditions so that the head of a family may be able to become a home-owner?
I say, at this point, that the government is certainly not doing what it should, not because it does not want to, but because it is prevented from doing so by this financial power. What I say today-and I am not afraid to say it-is that where financial matters are concerned, it is not the government that is leading. It is quite another system, and our governments are the victims thereof. There are men of good will among the ministers, but they are bound, hand and foot, and lack the possibility of enabling our Canadian families to get a home.
Let us consider once more the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act. I told you that I had spent the summer touring my constituency. In fact, I did more than that, for I came every week to Ottawa, endeavouring to solve such problems as were submitted to my attention. I also went to Quebec; in short, I travelled everywhere, trying to find out what was wrong.
Let me tell you about an experience I have had with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which experience floored me. C.M.H.C. now grants loans for the construction of old folks' homes. There again-I will prove to you that it is nothing but a smoke screen-they do not go about it directly but in a round about way.
Out of 11 applications in our area in the last two or three years, only one home was

built. Only one, and even at that, those who were granted the authorization to build it had to fight to the last. One! Yet we pay people, bureaucrats to attend to the needs of the people. The second permit was held up- was blocked, in common language-for two years. The people responsible for organizing the benevolent association had gone from door to door and collected $17,000 to build that home. Then, for two years, those $17,000 were frozen there, all plans held up, and things got to the point where it was decided not to build.
Well, when the people decided to come and see me, I told them: "Friends, let us take the bull by the horns." I went to Ottawa to see what had been done. I went to the office in Hull, to see what was going on in the province of Quebec. I also looked into what was being done in Ontario. I went to Quebec because we are dealing with a joint plan. Talk about joint plans: the federal government says: See Quebec about it. Quebec says: See the federal government. I therefore went to all concerned.
And do you know what I found out? That the federal office in Chicoutimi was holding up the works. I can give you the name of the manager of that office if you want it. I even told him: "Your name has never been given out in the house; be careful that it is not."

The Quebec norm was established at $5,000, probably because the cost of living is higher in Ontario-I do not know-and in that province, they are entitled to build nicer houses than in Quebec. The norm was $7,000 per bed in Ontario and $5,000 in Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister most sincerely, and as a matter of fact, I left my friend in Chicoutimi with these words: If I am unable to obtain from your office, I am sure that the minister will make them available to me. And I am still waiting for that information in order to complete my investigation and find out exactly what went wrong. We finally reached the construction stage, after a delay of two years and a half, not because of the head office here in Ottawa or of the Quebec office, but because of a small local office. A great many things are going to happen, because there are still ten applications from my area and others will keep coming in.
Homes for older persons are urgently needed in my district and I feel that in the future there should not be a two years' delay after an application has been received to have it approved. This is a proof, as I said earlier, that certain means are resorted to in order to thwart the object of the legislation for the construction of homes for older citizens and which is in fact almost perfect. Another piece of legislation which is a smoke screen is the one providing for a $30 monthly increase for old age pensioners.
All the newspapers announced that the old people would receive $30. That is another new piece of legislation, as reported in the newspapers, but what is it, really? Everybody will have to pay more taxes for the benefit of 24 or 25 per cent of the population, although we were told that all senior citizens would benefit from this allowance. I know old people who receive $1, $2 or $3 per month; you go and talk to them and you will see that they are aware of the effects of the act. And all this was anticipated, as I have said when the bill was passed; however, it was passed just to add one more act to the statutes.
And it was the same with the Canada Pension Plan, the very same thing: always to get more, levy another tax, and fleece the sheep a little closer!

For instance, take the case of a young man, aged 18; at first, he will pay $156 per year into the pension plan at age 18, and at age 65, if you add it up,-I did it during the holidays,-if, for 45 years, he pays $156 per year at a yearly interest rate of 6%, which is loaned at 6% yearly, after 45 years, his total contribution will be $35,000, and for what? A monthly pension of $104! Not even the total interest on the $35,000 that he would now be able to draw.
It is the man who lives to the age of 65 who will benefit. Again, this is not an act to provide security, but to tax the individual's security, to fleece him afterwards. If at least, the same efforts were made to find ways of getting money out of the pockets of rich people who exploit the country night and day, who pay $1 for what is worth $1,000, in brief, if our leaders racked their brains as much to And out or ferret out the hideouts where banks, for instance, stash away their secret loot, or to tax large corporations who exploit our resources for which they paid nothing. For instance, in the province of Quebec, iron ore is given away at half a cent per ton and bought at $300. But there, governments remain silent as the grave, they do not dare say a word and that is where we see the secret power-and the stronger the power the more silent it is-which imposes its will upon our leaders.
It is not because Liberals are here today; leaders have always been the same. We were the victims of financial powers, and still are today. We still have men in the government; I have said so in the beginning. I do not wish to criticize men, for they are the victims and I pity them. As a matter of fact, they are the victims of this infernal system which reduces our people to slavery. They are victims, and that is why I am making a speech today; it is for the population as well as for parliament, for I am trying to shatter this power which extends from one ocean to the other.
I also said that our laws, apart from being a smokescreen, are a web of injustice. And to name only one, I will simply mention the Income Tax Act.
In a few days, I will have the opportunity of presenting a notice of motion on that very subject. I simply wish to speak about income tax, particularly as it affects the worker and as opposed to the exemptions from which companies, trusts and banks still benefit. The worker pays taxes on his gross salary, even

though he has four, five, six and seven children to feed. The income tax is deducted right off, without his permission being asked. His daily bread is taken away, while trusts and large companies benefit from generous deductions.
For several years now, for example, we have asked for a reduction in the income tax paid by lumbermen. Nowadays they need a power saw and safety equipment, and they have to travel. The government has been asked to allow these workers to deduct from their income tax the price of their power saws and all their working equipment, as well as the maintenance costs which often reach $500, $600 or even $700.
Domtar enjoys tax exemptions for maintenance and every imaginable and possible depreciation on stationary machinery. A $400 or $500 tax deduction is asked for the head of a family who goes to break his back in the bush, a deduction of $500, $600 or $700 to buy his tools and pay his travelling expenses: No, it is impossible.
It is unfair. When a self-employed individual files his tax return at the end of the year, he will make every deduction he can and hide everything he can. That is all right, but the worker will be fleeced every week without the right to complain. If he does not submit, he will be thrown in jail. Do you not see the inequity of this legislation?
We had to put up with quite a lot; no wonder the people are dissatisfied. Do not play the hypocrites. You know it as well as I do.
The people are dissatisfied because their representatives are not acting in their best interests and fail to perform their duty as members of the House of Commons, that is, to protect society.
I wish that those words be mulled over not only by the people, but by all members. I ask them to examine their conscience in an attempt to come down to earth and to put the general interest before private interest.
This is what I was told by a great parliamentarian upon my arrival in parliament. It struck me and it is true. Here, we must first and foremost, in every area, whether a labour question or something else, make sure that the general interest comes first.
Well, I say that, particularly in the financial field, the general interest, the welfare of the people must come before the interest of any individual whether it is a trust, a bank, a chartered bank, or whatever it is. It is our

duty to defend the welfare of the people against these hidden powers.
