Discussion on Housing
It is conservatively estimated that we shall need about a million new homes in Canada in the next seven years. With costs of construction and materials increasing year by year, this means an investment within the next seven years of between $12 billion to $15 billion to provide our people with adequate and proper shelter. How are we to meet this goal? Certainly not by increasing interest rates. These rates have risen from 5 per cent to 8J per cent in the last few years. The government is specifically responsible for this problem and it must find the solution to it. A way must be found to finance home construction in Canada. I submit that the government would be well advised to seek a new approach to the housing question.
Housing is so important for the welfare of our people that the needs of the housing industry for money should not be met on the open market where high interest rates are charged. Housing capital cannot be placed in the same category as investment capital which will provide a return when the investment develops. The sooner we realize that housing capital falls into a category different from investment and resource capital, the sooner we shall find a new approach to the problem. The money required for housing ought to be given special consideration so far as interest rates are concerned. I therefore suggest to the minister that he would be well advised to set up a national housing fund. It should be a revolving fund, with the money that is paid back on home mortgages being lent again to provide more capital for more new houses.

Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question? Does he not know that that is what happens now, that all the money that comes back on housing loans goes right into new housing in addition to the hundreds of millions of dollars more provided each year by government and parliamentary action?

Yes, I am aware of that, but the minister refers to something that is slightly different from my suggestion. The operation of the present policy is not adequate. Initially this revolving fund ought to have not less than $5 billion. Some of that money will return as mortgages are paid and will be returned in new loans. If it is found after a period of years, that this fund is not sufficient, then possibly $500 million a year through private investment might be put into this field. The revolving aspect of the fund would grow year by year, keeping pace with the need for new housing.

[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Certain government moneys or certain areas of government income ought to be used to provide money for this fund. It seems to me that resource development income is a legitimate type of income which, so far as government is concerned, could well be transferred to another type of resource investment. Certainly there is no more important kind of resource investment than housing. But beyond this it seems to me that money must be provided for housing investment at low interest. It would not be unreasonable if the government in setting up the kind of fund I am talking about would consider an interest rate of 2 per cent or 3 per cent per year.
As the policy of the government builds up year by year a greater obligation in foreign investment we are giving soft loans to foreign countries over long periods, up to 50 years, and charging no interest at all. In some areas this soft loan investment or aid to foreign countries is merely carrying a service charge of approximately half of one per cent. If this is necessary to aid developing countries in other parts of the world I am not against the policy. It is a legitimate type of aid. But how much more necessary it is to have a similar policy in Canada to meet an urgent need. We need an urgent aid program ourselves because if we do not do anything we shall blunder along as we are at present, with the housing backlog year by year becoming greater than it was the previous year.
I am not making an unreasonable suggestion. A previous speaker pointed out that if a war broke out in which Canada found itself necessarily involved there would be no question but that we would have to get the money to finance the war. To compare a war situation with a housing situation may seem farfetched, but the crisis and the need are just the same so far as our economy and the welfare of the Canadian people are concerned.
In this connection my mind goes back to world war II. I believe it was in 1943 that the then minister of finance, Mr. Ilsley, announced a large loan to finance the war effort. Nobody in the House of Commons raised any objection because the urgency and the need for the money were evident. Nevertheless a question was asked of Mr. Ilsley as to how much he was paying as interest on the money. The answer was three-quarters of 1 per cent. He was then asked how it was, when the average interest rate was 4 per cent or 5 per cent, that he could get money at
October 2, 1967

three quarters of 1 per cent. His reply was: "That is what it cost. In view of the war effort and the crisis we are in, why should we pay more than it cost?"
If we could finance the war effort with money at that rate, then it seems to me that money to meet the housing crisis in Canada should be available at less than 8J per cent. It seems to me it would be a good policy if the Bank of Canada were used to provide the part of this fund, say half a billion dollars a year, that is not available from some special source of income such as I referred to previously. If this were done a $12,000 home would not cost $25,000 at the end of a 20-year purchase period. The cost would be cut from $25,000 to $15,000 or $16,000.
My point in bringing this up this afternoon is simply to emphasize the fact that it is not good enough to go along in the manner in which we have been proceeding during the past few years. Each year the backlog becomes greater. Each year the need becomes more imperative and yet each year the only alternative seems to be to raise interest rates and thus put the increasing cost of acquiring homes on the shoulders of the people who can least afford it.
I strongly urge the minister that in his consultations with his cabinet colleagues he see to it that the government comes up with a different approach to the question of financing home construction. As long as this is not done it seems to me it will be impossible for anyone on this side of the house to express confidence in the government on this kind of issue, simply because the facts are so clearly before us.
That is the gist of what I wanted to say, Mr. Speaker. In summary, what we are being offered today as a solution to the housing problem is inadequate, and the problem will continue to grow, as it has for the last number of years, until it reaches a point where it will become impossible to solve. I suggest that a new approach be taken. I suggest that we stop fiddling around with policies that over and over again have proven to be unable to meet the need.
We should use our own resources to provide the homes that we need. We have the building materials. We have the cement and the gravel to provide the foundations for basements. We have building materials in ample abundance to build not one million homes in the next ten years but two million homes if necessary. We have the tools, the manpower and the know-how. Why can we not do it? It is because we are tied to an
Discussion on Housing antiquated financial policy totally inadequate to fulfil our potential. Surely there ought to be something better. I realize it is a difficult problem for the minister but I hope he will take the lead in providing an alternative policy to what he is now suggesting.

Mr. Speaker, in debating the amendment before us we are dealing with something fundamental for all Canadians, the need for shelter and decent housing. As the director of the special project on low income housing for the Canadian Welfare Council put it in a recent speech, "House and home stand at the centre of people's lives."
Listening to the remarks of the spokesman for the official opposition and to those of other members who have participated in the debate, one would have thought it would have been better if more time had been devoted to analysing our present situation with respect to what could be done about the availability and the cost of housing, as well as our ability to provide the funds, both from government and from the private sector, in order to do as much as is necessary to make sure our people have available to them decent housing at a cost they can afford. However, listening in particular to the remarks of the spokesman for the official opposition it seemed to me he attempted to dwell more on the past, and his analysis was based more on trying to attribute blame and find reasons for failure with respect to the present situation.
Because of the approach adopted by the mover of the amendment it is at least in part necessary for us to look back over the same period of time, and when we do that we must carry out a somewhat similar analysis. But first of all I would like to draw to the attention of the house the inconsistency and contradiction which lie behind the presentation of the amendment, an inconsistency and a contradiction so great that the seemingly attractive wording of the amendment do not make up for them, with the result that it seems to me that reasonable and fairminded people in this house, no matter what their concern about the housing situation may be, could not possibly support the amendment.

Discussion on Housing words, the spokesman for the official opposition in effect is saying that the government has aggravated the situation by spending money on youth allowances, student loans, payments to the dairy industry and increased old age pensions for our senior citizens. He is saying we have aggravated the situation by spending more money on incentives to help areas of slow growth and industrial recession. In effect the official opposition is saying that we have aggravated the situation by tripling the amount-$900 million has been spent in 1967-spent on housing by this government over that spent by the official opposition when it was in office. That is the reason that today they are in the position where they belong, in the opposition.
The official opposition is now saying that we should eliminate or cut back the programs we have put into effect. These are programs which we presented to this parliament. In the main they were supported by the official opposition. On a number of occasions they even called upon us to accelerate the timing of these measures. Are they in effect saying that we should cut out the youth allowances, the studen loans, the incentives to industry and slow growth areas? Are they saying we should eliminate the guaranteed income supplement for older Canadians? This would appear to be a not unreasonable analysis of what the spokesman for the official opposition had to say in putting forward his amendment this afternoon.
The usual nonsense.

Are they saying we should not have trebled the spending on housing since the present government took office in 1963? This also seemed to be implicit in the argument put forward in respect of the amendment which is before us.
The spokesman for the official opposition has spoken critically of the borrowing and the deficits of this government. A large proportion of the borrowing has been necessary in part to raise money for housing. Had this money not been spent there would be a much worse situation in respect of housing than there is today. I might add that these comments about deficits came from a very good source, because no other group in this house has a greater knowledge of deficits and how to create them than the official opposition. The difference between the deficits of their day and what we may have now is that their deficits did not come about through a program to increase the growth of the country, to increase jobs or housing starts in this (Mr. Gray.]
country. They came about through mismanagement. This is something which was recognized at the polls by the voters of this country.
Get down to facts and stop talking about the past.

If members of this house and the public wish to pursue the same type of analysis made the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Chatterton) and develop it, they will come to the conclusion that at least in part with respect to our present housing situation one cannot overlook as a cause the neglect, lack of concern and lack of priorities on the part of the official opposition when it had the opportunity as the government of this country to deal with this problem.
It seems to me that a prime reason for the efforts we have been making and must continue to make is that we have to deal with a problem which accumulated when the need for housing of all types was not dealt with by the previous government in any way which could be termed even slightly effective. The building which should have been carried out, the planning which should have been undertaken and the projects which should have been under way between 1957 and 1962 were not carried out. Certainly it is obvious, at least in my opinion, that the present government has to deal not only with the matter of our growing economy and growing population at the present time but also has to make up for what was not done between 1957 and 1962.
Let me attempt to buttress this point by citing some examples. Did the previous government pass legislation to make possible federal loans covering 90 per cent of the cost of public housing for families and senior citizens? Did it make possible National Housing Act loans for older homes? Did it increase to the present level of $18,000 the maximum amount available through N.H.A. mortgage loans? Did it increase by billions of dollars the total amount available through C.M.H.C. for housing and urban renewal programs? Did it take the initiative which led to the creation of the provincial housing corporations in most of the provinces and which over the past few years has enabled the provinces to take care of their constitutional responsibilities in this field more adequately? The answer is obvious. The previous government did none of these things. These things came into effect only after the present government took office.
October 2, 1967

Let me cite an example in my area of Windsor. The people in this area know very well the situation with which they had to contend before the present government took office in 1963. The present government certainly did make efforts in this regard which were very successful in helping to overcome the unemployment and lack of growth that prevailed during the years of office of the previous government. I am informed that since September of 1965 695 public housing units for families and senior citizens have been or are almost completed. In the years between 1957 and 1962 only one project of some 137 units was planned and built. If I am not mistaken, almost half of the public housing units in the city of Windsor today came about through the initiative and legislation in the matter of housing of the present government.
There has been a lot of talk about housing starts and certainly there is justifiable concern about the level of starts this year and what may happen in the coming year. I was informed this afternoon that while housing starts in the Windsor area from January to August, 1966 totalled 761 the number of starts in the same period this year totalled 928. I am not suggesting there is not still a lot more to be done both in the Windsor area and across the country to help provide adequate and decent housing at reasonable cost for the people of this country, but I certainly think it is wrong to urge, as the spokesman for the opposition did in presenting his amendment to us, that it should be adopted and, in other words, the government defeated.
I am one of those, Mr. Speaker, who call for increased federal initiative and activity in the housing area, but at the same time I cannot ignore the fact, under our existing constitutional arrangements, of provincial responsibility and jurisdiction. While calling for greater federal concern and initiative, I think it is also very important at this time to call for greater provincial concern and responsibility when it comes to operating in this vital area of national policy.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Let me cite some examples. In June of 1966 the Ontario Housing Corporation carried out a survey in the Windsor area in respect of housing needs. One of the recommendations which resulted from this survey was that in each of the years 1966 and 1967 a total of 350 units of public housing-300 family units and 50 senior citizen units-would be sufficient for the community's need. There have been 27053-1731
Discussion on Housing hundreds of applications filed with the housing authority, the city of Windsor building corporation, which is in large part responsible for senior citizen housing. The remarks in Windsor city council and by many others would certainly indicate that at the present time there is room in Windsor for a substantially greater effort in the public housing field, and certainly that is my view. However, at the same time, under our existing structure this is still a matter for initiative by the provincial government. I might say, and I will enlarge upon this later in my remarks, that in spite of the provincial constitutional position there is room at the present time for greater federal initiative. The point I am trying to make is that even taking these facts into account, under the existing laws and the existing financial arrangements in the province of Ontario and across this country, provincial governments at this time could be doing a lot more than they are doing to help alleviate the present housing situation.
Let me mention another matter which perhaps has a more local application. There is a public housing project being constructed at this time in the Bloomfield road area of Windsor. At one point, although a number of these units had been completed permission was not granted by the Ontario Housing Corporation for occupation by families that had been assigned to them. The explanation given was that even though the units themselves had been completed the landscaping had not been finished and the sidewalks were not laid. I wonder about a provincial government which, even though it may have had the best of motivations, seems to put greater importance on landscaping, lawns and sidewalks than the basic need for shelter.
Let me refer to another point which seems to me to deserve much greater importance than it receives at this time. There is a lot more room for effort by provincial governments to take advantage of existing legislation in order to carry out greater and more numerous projects of land assembly. One of the problems referred to in the debate today and last week is that relating to the cost of land. Certainly there is room for greater activity in the federal-provincial land assembly area. This means at this time greater activity by provincial governments which would have some positive effect on the availability of land at a reasonable cost. If properly serviced land is not available in this way, this undoubtedly is a factor which creates a serious effect on the cost of housing.

Discussion on Housing
Just another lecture to the provinces. You are hiding behind the constitution again.

I do not suggest that the present distribution of powers in respect of responsibility as to some matters of social welfare is a distribution which brings about the most effective solution to these problems under twentieth century conditions, but the constitution as interpreted by the courts exists and it is simply not fair to the public to say-I am trying to use moderate language-that this constitutional division of responsibility between provincial and federal governments does not exist.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
I will answer questions when I have completed my remarks.
Is this crisis not of national concern?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, and of provincial concern.

I will deal with this aspect later in my remarks. As the hon. member suggests, it is of national concern, but it is also of provincial and local concern. I do not hesitate to say, as I have said already, that it is one in respect of which the federal government must be prepared to take immediate and ever-increasing initiatives in line with its present abilities to find a method of carrying out this and other programs which the people of Canada expect.

speechtext: That is what the amendment suggests.

There has been a lot of comment today and last week about the increase in the N.H.A. interest rate. It should again be stressed that this rate is the maximum rate of interest which can be charged for mortgages insured under the National Housing Act. There may be arguments about the effect of this rate, and certainly they must be considered, but often this change is referred to in terms which seem to indicate that the government has fixed the rate at 8J per cent for all National Housing Act mortgages. That is simply not the case. Surely it is in order to stress again that the government has not decreed that all National Housing Act mortgages should bear 8J per cent interest, even though I agree there may be some argument about the effect of this step.

The aim of the government, as I understand it, is to encourage a range of rates below the 8J- per cent ceiling in order to provide more funds from the private sector and, hopefully, lower rates for housing purposes through market forces. At the end of last week, and I speak subject to correction, the Bank of Montreal indicated that its mortgages for housing would be available at the rate of 7| per cent. If that is correct it would indicate that, rather than having created a single fixed rate for all mortgages in the housing field, the action of the government is a step toward its goal of providing a range of rates below 8J per cent for housing mortgages. It is hoped that in many areas of the country this rate will be well below the 8^ per cent maximum. Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this house recessed at six o'clock I was pointing out that
October 2, 1967

the government had merely made the 8i per cent rate the maximum rate and had not moved, as some have attempted to suggest, to make it the sole rate for insured lending under the National Housing Act. At the same time, while recognizing that the government's intentions in making this move were of the best, with the aim of attempting to attract more private funds into the home mortgage market, I wish to make clear that in my opinion raising the ceiling of the interest rate in this way is at most a partial and an incomplete answer to the need for more housing. It is certainly not the answer for those earning $8,000 a year or less.
The government must be prepared to take further initiatives to assist people with moderate and lower incomes to have decent housing, in addition to the steps already taken which I referred to earlier in my remarks. This must be done if private enterprise cannot or will not do the job adequately. The Windsor Star, in a recent editorial which I must admit was not particularly favourable to the change in the maximum rate, made this point:
It is a curious feature of our economy that money seemingly is available for almost everything but that which is most needed. It's apparently possible to get money for new supermarkets, sky-scraping office buildings, etc., but not for homes for the people.
This illustrates once again that our private enterprise system has failed lamentably in the post-war period in the field of housing. The situation is acute and becoming more so. It would be quite desperate were it not for governmental housing developments, subsidies, etc.
The editorial reads in part:
It may be the day is coming when most housing will be built by public enterprise. Housing will be provided by governments, just as educating, water, police and fire protection and many other essentials now are provided.
The editorial, at another point, reads:
This is just another example of governmental intervention brought about by failure of private enterprise to meet public needs.
I have said that the change in the maximum rate cannot be the sole answer to the need for more housing. However, I recognize the significance of the situation surrounding the federal government's present borrowing ability. It will help no one Mr. Speaker, to call for measures which would worsen this situation and which would make it more difficult for the federal government to finance its activities at this time.
I think that measures calling for increased borrowing at this time will increase the upward pressure on interest rates, the present
Discussion on Housing levels of which are of concern to many. This will lead to increasing inflationary pressures which hurt everyone, especially those with lower incomes. The other side of the coin, of course, is that the public at large is concerned about the present level and burden of taxation; and, of course, taxation is obviously the government's only other immediate source of funds.
We must act responsibly to improve this situation, so we will be in a position to move ahead in the housing area as quickly as possible in ways that may call for further expenditure. In the meantime we must spend the moneys the federal government has available in ways that provide the most to areas of greatest immediate need in housing. The federal government must be prepared not only to explore but to move into new areas both with existing funds and funds which may be raised in the future, to ensure the filling of the basic need for housing, something which is coming to be considered, if it is not already considered, a basic right of Canadians.
While recognizing provincial constitutional responsibility-and I referred to this question earlier in my remarks-I think there is room at this time for greater federal initiative and action. I think the time has come for a federal minister having as his sole responsibility federal government action in the field of housing and urban affairs. I believe there is a great deal to be said for the suggestion made by the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn), calling for the creation of special house building corporations in effective partnership with the provinces, if possible, or under federal auspices alone, if necessary, to build houses at reasonable cost as was done by the wartime housing corporation.
I believe the emergency is of such proportions, in spite of the efforts taken and the achievements that have resulted through measures to which I referred earlier, that this type of initiative could be justified and could very well be supported in the event of a test being made of the constitutional question. I think, too, that the time has come to explore making mortgages available, either by allocating a portion of our existing funds or other funds that will be raised in future, directly by the federal government with interest rates subsidized by the federal government, to people with lower incomes.
Certainly, it is time we reached the situation where there is government action, federal government action if necessary, in partnership with the provinces if possible, to buy

October 2, 1967
Discussion on Housing and hold-to stockpile, in other words-land across the country to help eliminate speculation and profiteering in land. This is something which in my opinion creates unjustifiable pressures on the cost of land and is a vital factor in the question of the cost of housing today.
Also, Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the time has not come to consider the possibility of creating disincentives to private builders who prefer to concentrate on office buildings and luxury dwellings rather than doing more in the field of private homes.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
While calling on this government to do more in the field of housing, I certainly would say that this government, contrary to what has been suggested by hon. members opposite, has not failed to recognize the nature of the problem in the country. It has worked to deal with it, and definite progress has been made. What this government has accomplished in this area in the past I think justifies my belief that it deserves the continued confidence of this house and this country with respect to its ability to go on and do even more in this vital field of national policy. This fact also justifies the rejection by this house of the amendment before it.
The adoption by this house of the amendment would do nothing to help the present situation. The amendment will change no existing law. It will bring about the passing of no new law. It will not add one dollar to the money already available for housing. It will cause not one more house to be built. It will only bring about another election which will cause uncertainty and delay in the taking of further steps to provide more housing at reasonable cost. I think that in any event the people of this country are in a position to judge the ability of the present government to do a more effective job in the field of housing as compared with the ability of the parties opposite to do the same. Certainly, as I pointed out at the beginning of my remarks, there is nothing that the official opposition were able to accomplish during their period of office which would cause anyone in this house or in this country to take the wording of their amendment as seriously as they hope.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I welcome the opportunity of being able to enter this debate. First of all, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Chatterton) upon the amendment he proposed. I should like also to state that on Thursday night of last week when the house was about to close I had the opportunity, after having heard the statement by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) on the previous day, to make a few comments. At that time I mentioned the fact that even in the city of London, the riding which I have the pleasure to represent, we are short of some 4,000 dwelling units at the present time. This represents a considerable crisis. It has been reliably stated also that at the present time we are short of some 250,000 units across Canada.
I was rather surprised to hear some of the statements made by the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Gray) because I consider him a good friend of mine. I thought he was somewhat above making some of the partisan statements he made. I do not think it was necessary for him to make them. Our function in the house is to try and get along together. It is the function of the members of the official opposition to put forward ideas which we believe to be in the best interests of the country. The hon. member attacked the former administration and at the same time kept repeating that the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich was thinking in terms of the last year and of previous years. Yet, the same hon. member spoke about the previous administration in a way which I do not think contributed a great deal to the well-being of this house or to the well-being of parliament. I wonder if perhaps some of the remarks he made might not have been the product of a guilty conscience. However, we will leave that for what it may be.
The announcement made by the minister the other evening that the interest rate would be increased to a maximum of 8.25 per cent came, I am sure, as quite a blow to many of us. Many people who think in terms of the general good of Canada-and I do not mean to imply that the minister is not because I know him to be the kind of person who does-think of doing those things which are best not necessarily for their own party but for the country. I recognize the minister to be a great Canadian. Tonight, I am concerned about an item which appeared in a newspaper. I will not read it. Let me say only that it
October 2, 1967

related to an $18,000 mortgage. The newspaper stated that by the time a person has paid off this mortgage, the amount of money that he would have repaid would have totalled $42,000, including interest. This is a fantastic amount of money with which to saddle a younger person or even an older person. We find that a person wishing to buy a house costing that much would have to pay in the neighbourhood of $1,000 a year in interest. I wonder whether this would not make private ownership of a dwelling an uneconomic proposition. This is something about which we should think. There was a time when we used to encourage the young people of this country to acquire a home of their own. It used to be our feeling that in so doing we were at least going through the motion of encouraging them to be better citizens. We used to think that owning a home gave us a stake in the community, made us feel we were part of the overall picture. It was our feeling that it made better citizens of us.
I recall the time when I purchased my first home. At that time I think the down payment was $300, and I felt very proud of the fact that I had a stake in the community in which I was privileged to live.
Let us think for a moment about the penalties which we are forcing on prospective home owners today. First, let us think of the interest which they have to pay for 25 years, which may amount to $24,000. To that we must add the 11 per cent tax on building materials-and I do not intend to comment on whether this is good or bad at the moment-or another $1,800. Then, let us think of the average increase in property taxes in urban areas. This adds another $300 for the duration of this program, which comes to another $7,500. These people were fortunate enough to be able to pay $10,000 down, and there are few who can. If you add that to the figures I have already mentioned you will come up with something in the neighborhood of $43,300 which they would be paying just for the privilege of having a stake in the community.
These are some of the things that I am concerned about, and I think everyone in this house should be very disturbed about these impediments that we are throwing in the way of the young people particularly. There are other factors such as land values which are escalating all the time. They are part of the inflationary tendency. This is a further handicap which we are putting in the way of these people.
Discussion on Housing
However, let us look at the problem from another angle. Suppose these people do not own a home. They are, nevertheless faced with the law of business balance, so they must pay higher rent because naturally the value of a home on which owners must pay up to 8.25 per cent will go up and therefore the value of replacement homes will go up. The value of the home which a person is renting will go up, and therefore he will have to pay more by way of rental.
This is a very serious situation, particularly for the young people who are raising a family. These are some of the things that contribute to the ever increasing inflationary pressures.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Let us consider, for instance, the minimum income factor of $8,000 that was mentioned. What about the lower income earner, the man who, let us say, earns $5,000 a year and is paying $75 to $100 per month rent for his home? This man cannot qualify for this type of mortgage. The result is that when his rent goes up he will be paying more money just to subsidize those people in the $8,000 and over income bracket. Is this man not worthy of consideration, or is he supposed to be some kind of second class citizen? Is he not entitled to the dignity of the individual? The same inflationary pressures are going to send his rent up, and I ask the government what it intends to do in such a situation. I feel that these are the people we should be assisting. Of that I am sure, because I lived on that kind of income for many years. It is the man in the lower income group for whom we should have a program.
Let me mention for a moment, Mr. Speaker, something that has been referred to in this house many times, namely the 11 per cent tax on building materials which is collected by the Department of National Revenue at great expense and lent back again through the N.H.A. at a lesser interest rate. I should like to know the actual net figure derived from this tax on building materials. How much does it cost us to administer the tax? For example, how much does the book work cost? How much does it cost the supplier of building materials and the builder himself to handle the administrative work? All of these expenses, which are legitimate expenses, are charged against the company concerned, if these charges are exempt from tax this just means that the government derives even less tax in each particular case.

October 2, 1967
Discussion on Housing
The net amount received from this tax has been reliably estimated to be in the neighbourhood of 2| per cent of the full tax, yet these people must pay the full tax of 11 per cent. This is another obstacle tossed in the way, particularly of our young people today who want a home of their own.
I would ask whether this permitted increase in the interest rate that the minister has mentioned will make it possible for people to build, or will it make it impossible? Will it mean that eventually the private dwelling will become an uneconomic unit and that it will not be reasonable for a person to think in terms of building a home for himself? I am sure that every member in this chamber is well aware that this situation will place the lower income family right in the middle of another inflationary squeeze.
We are subsidizing, Mr. Speaker, such persons as the wheat farmers and the dairy farmers. We also subsidize the coal industry. I do not disapprove of this; indeed, I think it is all to the good. In view of the fact that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) found himself in a very embarrassing position vis-a-vis the wheat farmers, I think the government had to subsidize them. But why do we not think in terms of protecting the jewels of our society? Why do we not think of protecting those people in the lower income brackets so that they can qualify for a mortgage to build a home of their own?
I contend that if we made it possible for people in the wage bracket of between $5,000 to $7,000 or $8,000 to qualify for a mortgage to build a home of their own, first of all we would be making better Canadians. As I said a moment ago we would give such persons a stake in their community. I suggest that we should do some very real thinking along the line of making it possible for people within that income bracket to obtain a mortgage at an interest rate of 5 per cent.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, we are not above subsidizing our own people in order to help them out, particularly those in the younger age groups starting a family. It does not make sense for them to live in the low-cost housing developments that we have; they want a place of their own where the kiddies can romp about outside in the back yard, be it big or small. I know from experience that this is important to such people.
I should like to impress upon the government at this time the importance of doing something to help the people in that wage bracket. These young people are Canada's greatest asset. During the war it was the

young people who were sent overseas to fight for us; I think it is now time we did a little bit of fighting for them.
It is true that some of these people will never own a home; that has always been true. But are we going to condemn them to live in these low-cost public housing developments? These developments do not harmonize with the outlook of young people with a young and growing family. We grant loans to foreign developing countries interest-free, yet we forget the most important asset that we have in our own country.
Let us look at the situation objectively, Mr. Speaker. This morning I called on two banking institutions. Not too long ago it was possible to obtain a mortgage from these institutions at the rate of 7 per cent, though I admit they were selective in placing those mortgages. I asked the manager of one of these institutions this morning what they were charging at the moment, and he told me it was 8 per cent. I contend that that is the thin edge of the wedge, and that within a very short space of time they will increase that rate to the maximum amount of 8-J per cent. I asked him whether that would be the case, but he replied he did not know.
Supposing, Mr. Speaker, this does happen and these rates do go up to 8J per cent. Are the institutions that lend money for this purpose going to lend money at a lesser rate for commercial purposes? We will also find a restraint in the business community. The prices of all other homes are going to increase correspondingly. Let us say that a house is built today for $20,000 and the amount of $20,000 is paid in interest over the term of the mortgage. At the former rate of interest the same house may still have cost $20,000 to build but the interest would have amounted, say, to $12,000. This means that the price of the house has risen by $8,000. The effect of these increases will be felt all the way down to the man who is paying $75 a month rent. That rent will be increased perhaps to $100 a month. This fellow who is making, shall we say, $100 a week will pay an increased rent, according to inflationary trends, perhaps of $115 or $120. The time when he can buy his own home will be postponed. Perhaps he will be too old to qualify for a mortgage when he has saved the money. [DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
It is this point with which I am concerned. I am speaking on behalf of the little man who goes to work every day and carries a lunch pail. He is the man in my mind because he
October 2, 1967

makes this country great. I implore the government tonight to do something to assist him and others like him. Let us help them reach the goals aspired to by good Canadians.
Charity begins at home. I do not say that we should stop the great work we are doing for some developing nations, but let us look at home first. Let us protect those who are the very jewels of this country in which we are privileged to live.
One might ask, where are we to get the money? I say that the first place we ought to look is at our bureaucracy. We ought to cut down the amount of bureaucracy in this country. Perhaps we could cut down on the empire building that has been going on, shall we say, from 1939, I am not excepting the former administration because this is no time to be political and we ought to call a spade a spade. We serve in this house first as Canadians and secondly as party members. As I say, if we can cut down on bureaucracy, it would be all to the good.
I wish to read from the editorial page of the Stratford Beacon Herald of August 1, 1967. Hon. members may not be familiar with this newspaper which is published about 40 miles from the riding I have the privilege to represent. The article reads:
An Ottawa report setting forth the average income of income taxpayers in Canadian cities was published in this newspaper a few days ago. Average income reported by taxpayers in a number of Western Ontario cities, including Stratford, St. Thomas, Woodstock, Galt and Owen Sound, was in the $4,500-4,700 bracket. In smaller or less industrialized centres the average would be lower. Beacon Herald Ottawa correspondent Richard Jackson, in more than one of his columns, has discussed the civil service salaries ranging, for senior officials, from $18,000 to $35,000, with a few drawing more.
The Ottawa correspondent earlier this year had reported 372,890 persons in the federal public service,-
That is 372,890 persons, Mr. Speaker, a fantastic figure.
-as it is now called, with a payroll of $2,063,892,000, not including the armed forces. It is taking one of every four tax dollars to provide this payroll. If one of these Western Ontario taxpayers reporting around $4,500 income was married, had one dependent, paid union dues and made some charitable donations, he might pay $160 income tax, of which $40 would go to pay federal employees receiving, in general, far more than the taxpayer.
Of course, the comparison is not really accurate; every taxpayer indirectly pays customs duties and federal sales tax on goods purchased, and this would make up part of his $40. It is also the case that civil servants in the higher salary brackets pay far more income tax. The important fact remains that we have 10 times as many people in the public service as in 1939-
Discussion on Housing
Ten times as many. Mr. Speaker, these are astounding figures:
-an increase out of all relation to population rise, taxpayers' incomes or anything else except the proliferation of Government departments. Ten times as many persons means far more than 10 times the salary total, because of increases granted from time to time since 1939. I would like to come back to the problem that is facing us and to say something about its nature. The first problem we have to deal with, if we are going to face up to the housing problem adequately and not in a partisan fashion, looking at the realities of the situation, is the shortage of capital or I might say, if you want to put it another way, the shortage of savings. Housing takes not only labour and materials, and at this point may I say we can help to improve the supply of both. Even the federal government has a role to play in this, and many of the efforts that have been made by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mar-chand) in recent years and months will, I believe, help to improve that situation.
We can also, I believe, improve our building methods. But housing also takes capital in the form of savings. Most buyers of housing are unable to pay cash. Most of them require to borrow some money to build houses, and therefore someone else must have savings in order to enable them to buy houses at the time they want them.
It is the savings to finance the purchase and rental of housing which are scarce today and, I have every reason to think, are likely to be scarce over the next few years. Housing must compete for capital with industry, and it must compete for capital with governments. We must have capital to provide jobs in industry, and governments must have capital to provide the infrastructure, the roads, the schools and all the other things governments must provide if there are going to be cities fit to live in.

Canadian rates must be high enough in relation to those of the United States that they will attract into Canada the capital required to supply our deficiency. This is just a fact of life. There is nothing we can do about it unless we can increase our own savings, and I do not think they can be increased quickly enough to enable us to dispense with foreign capital. Therefore, our interest rates must bear a proper relationship to those in the United States. However, as I listened to the debate I have heard a diversity of views. At times, there seemed to be a degree of unanimity among the government supporters. They all seemed to be hiding behind that great shield of provincial rights and responsibilities. Apparently, in this manner they hoped to be able to avoid the true responsibility for this crisis which is, of course, the failure of the government to do anything realistic not only towards solving the housing crisis but towards solving the money crisis that is facing our country.
Surely, as has been pointed out by other hon. members on this side of the house, there exists not only a housing crisis but a crisis in monetary policy. This crisis has been intensified and prolonged by months of government ineptitude, government inaction and government fumbling which has led from crisis to crisis and from stopgap measure to stopgap measure. The government has been going to the cupboard for a bone with which perhaps to seduce the Canadian voter, but finally, like Mother Hubbard, they have found the cupboard bare. They have been caught up in a web spun by their own fingers. They have been trying desperately to extricate themselves by using the classic economic ploy that the interest rate is not sufficient to attract more money into the mortgage field, hoping desperately to save the situation. At the same time, there has been an attempt to rescue this government once again from the consequences of its own folly. But, Mr. Speaker, the question the people of Canada are asking is: will these measures work?
Let us look at the situation. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) has pointed out very forcefully that because of the high cost of building and the unavailability of mortgage money the average individual must look not toward home ownership but toward

This is the question: is it the responsibility of the government to gear the economy of our country to allow individuals to purchase their own homes if they so wish, or is it, as the minister implies, the responsibility of the government to control and decide the type of housing that each individual must have? Are we going to force the individual, by the inexorable pressure of adverse economic factors, to live, as I said before, like rabbits in warrens in government subsidized housing? As we listen to the various speakers on the government side we seem to be coming to the inescapable conclusion that the latter is the answer.

These were revisions undertaken by thoughtful ministers-one of them is sitting opposite in a somewhat different portfolio-such as Hon. J. Ilsley and others. The work that they did at the time, along with the members of the opposition, had the effect or producing bills which, with reference to their own particular problems, did a fairly adequate job. Surely, Mr. Speaker, the time has come once again for a massive revision, for a long and in depth look to be taken, as I said before, at the present act. I am, of course, aware of the revisions that were made in November 1966; but I feel that as a result of a very careful study the act may possibly be entirely different.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
After all, Mr. Speaker, what were the initial purposes of the National Housing Act? We know that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was a crown agency incorporated by act of parliament in 1945 to administer the National Housing Act and to co-ordinate activities in housing. We sometimes forget when we talk of provincial co-operation and otherwise, that authority over and responsibility for a variety of functions affecting housing is part of the duties of C.M.H.C., both in the long term as well as in meeting the immediate requirements of the country. C.M.H.C. has power to act as insurer of mortgage loans, as lender or investor of public funds, as a guarantor and owner of property and other assets.
Another thing which is forgotten is that C.M.H.C. also acts as a research agency in fields associated with housing, and it assists provinces and municipalities in many aspects of urban growth.
However, it seems to me that somewhere along the line something has been omitted. The government's aim through these successive housing acts has surely been to stimulate and supplement the market for housing, to increase the flow of mortgage money, and to encourage lenders to make loans on more favourable terms to prospective home owners. These have been the purposes of the acts, Mr. Speaker, but it seems that the government has forgotten them.
Looking at all of the suggestions which have been made to date, several facts have emerged quite clearly. First of all, nobody appears to have an absolute answer to the problem. It is surely self-evident, as I said

October 2, 1967
Discussion on Housing before, that the time has come to do away with stop-gap measures, to put an end to finger-in-the-dike policies. It is obvious that the time has now come to make a complete reappraisal of the situation. I am not talking of next month or at the end of the next quarter when the interest rate is reviewed; now is the time to set up a joint committee of the kind I have suggested with all the power and means to look into and report on every facet of the housing crisis in this country. Perhaps at the same time the committee can look into the real cause of the monetary crisis which has been brought on by the policies of the government opposite.
In this regard, Mr. Speaker, I have never attempted to lay the blame for the present situation totally at the feet of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson). However, I am sure he must share some of the blame along with the other members of the government of which he is part.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext: He has lost the fight.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext:
That is true. The minister is surely the prisoner of the economic policies of the government. I even noticed the manner in which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) talked, as though the policies and decisions that are going to be made were his, not those of the cabinet or government.
I am well aware that the measures proposed by the Minister of Labour are probably all he can manage in the present circumstances within the framework of the economic chains that bind him. But I am also aware, Mr. Speaker, that this government has failed miserably to take adequate steps to head off the economic crisis that has precipitated this debate in the house.
It is a funny thing, Mr. Speaker, but even as the Minister of Labour was making his announcement about the increased interest rates the other night, thus increasing housing costs for every Canadian, the Minister of Finance was making another speech in Rio de Janeiro to the International Monetary Fund about the decision of the government to increase Canadian foreign aid.
The Minister of Finance made a rather revealing statement, Mr. Speaker. He said:
This decision has only recently been reaffirmed despite the efforts which we shall be making by budgetary policies and otherwise to limit the upward pressures on costs and prices to which I have already referred.
I might say I have a copy of his speech before me; indeed, the minister referred to it earlier.
Just imagine, Mr. Speaker, one minister sitting in the House of Commons suggesting measures to increase costs for the average Canadian, while another minister a few thousand miles away is making a pious speech to other ministers of finance, suggesting that we in Canada are going to do everything we can to keep down prices. These two ministers did not even have the decency to make these statements on different days.
As reported at page 3 of his speech, the Minister of Finance said:
Canada has had its share of difficulties in finding the right combination of policies to achieve our various goals.
Then a little later on he said:
But It is clear that we have been more successful in maintaining economic growth than we have been in achieving stability of costs and prices. It is our purpose, however, to combine continued growth with price stability-indeed I doubt whether in the long run the one can be achieved without the other-and we intend to make use of every means available to us to restore the balance.
That sort of thing does make one wonder, Mr. Speaker.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, surely the time has come for a reappraisal of our national economic needs. For example, perhaps it is time to take another look at breaking with the fixed exchange rate system and supporting instead a floating rate. That has been suggested. Perhaps we, as a country, have been tied too long to the federal reserve system of the United States and this is the cause of our trouble. Certainly, some economists say it is.
I should like to see the government set up some sort of inquiry. I have suggested a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons. After all, if such a committee were able to do the kind of job done by the Senate committee on aging, their report would be very worth while indeed. Let the committee talk to the most knowledgeable men in the country. This is the least we can do for the poor taxpayer no longer able to afford to buy his own home and with no sign of any tax relief on the horizon.
You no doubt know the difference, Mr. Speaker, between the home owner in the United States and the home owner in Canada. In the United States the home owner can deduct interest and real estate taxes paid on his home from income tax. This encourages the person who rents to buy a home of his own since a saving is possible by way of tax deduction for his monthly interest payment,

October 2, 1967

But no such incentive is given Canadian taxpayers. In Canada, it is cheaper to rent than to buy, and that is certainly true.
If the truth were known, Mr. Speaker, I wonder how many members of the house have already received letters from their constituents in which they say, in effect, that they were going to buy a home but cannot now afford one. I would be very surprised if there was one member in this house who has not received one such letter. Most of us have received many. The impact of this increase is catastrophic, as I said before. I suggest the minister ask some of the people who work in the House of Commons what they think and how this will affect their desire to become homeowners; I think he will get quite a surprise.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
I ask this government to stop the finger-in-the-dike principle. Let it set up a committee to look at this question in depth and come up with real solutions. Let us put an end to having a crisis every few months. We do not want, as the Prime Minister said, a crisis so that we can deal with the situation more effectively. There is no need for this country to have a crisis economy. The time has come for common sense. I plead with the government to come to its senses and to come to the aid of the average Canadian who is in deep trouble now, financial and otherwise, as a result of the policies which the government has engendered.

Mr. Speaker, the debate to this point at least has made one thing clear, namely, that the problem of scarce housing is neither new nor confined to Canada. The quotation of the remarks of Mr. T. L. Church by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Brand) shows that this subject has busied the Parliament of Canada over many decades. But perhaps the highly publicized awareness of the importance of the problem is new. A provincial election is taking place in Ontario.
I do not think that the peculiar circumstances which have brought about this awareness should cause us to underestimate the genuine problem that exists in the field of housing.
An attempt has been made to suggest that the fourth annual review of the Economic Council of Canada berates the government for allowing a housing crisis to develop. Some of those making this attempt evidently have not read the review. This is quite evident in
Discussion on Housing the exchanges that took place in the committee of supply here, last Thursday, and more particularly, in those exchanges that took place at pages 2586 and 2587 of Hansard.
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Chatterton) in moving his motion, quoted part of the most relevant paragraph in the review. Since we are referring again and again to that paragraph I think it would be well to read it in its entirety. It begins at page 133, and reads as follows:
We estimate that by the end of the 1960's housing starts and completions in Canada will need to rise to annual levels of at least 200,000 units to fully meet the nation's requirements at that time. The increase in the number of new households in 1970 is estimated to account for some 140,000 of these requirements, based on the projections discussed in Chapter 3. In addition, we estimate that replacement demand will have risen to 50,000 units per year by 1970; this is the amount of new building necessary simply to keep the total housing stock intact after allowing for various removals of units from use due to the elimination of substandard housing, population shifts, and changing economic land uses from residential into commercial, industrial, traffic and other public uses. Finally, it is estimated that by 1970 total stock of vacant dwellings available on the housing market would have to increase by roughly 10,000 units per year to provide for a minimum stock of unoccupied housing required to accommodate the mobility of the population and to facilitate a smooth adjustment between the demand and supply for housing. In 1966, with a decline in housing construction under conditions of monetary restraint and reduced mortgage financing, available vacancies appear to have fallen to inappropriately low levels, especially in some of the larger urban areas such as Toronto.
That is the famous paragraph on which so much of our discussion has centered. Let us look at the situation about which the amendment of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich complains.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis), when she spoke earlier today, blurred the distinction between the field of public housing and certain other programs which are similar on the one hand and the field of approved-lender mortgages on the other. We must keep these distinctions clearly in mind because it is to the latter field, not the former, that the 8| per cent interest ceiling applies.
Under the amendments made by Parliament in 1964, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was authorized to make 90 per cent loans to provinces, municipalities or their agencies for public housing accommodation for low income families or individuals. Provision in those amendments was made for a program of land acquisition and servicing

October 2, 1967
Discussion on Housing for public housing purposes, and the corporation was permitted to make loans of up to 90 per cent for this purpose.
To take advantage of these provisions, the provinces had to set up housing corporations. Eight provinces have done this. I cannot help but think that the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway should have directed the brunt of her argument more directly to those at whom it should properly have been directed. Frankly, and of her own volition, she ought to have admitted that her own province, British Columbia, had not set up a housing corporation and that some of the difficulties of which she complained could be attributed to this fact. In other words, Mr. Speaker, I think she ought to have been as rough with the Social Credit people as she was with the Liberals.
The corporations in the eight provinces were set up in the period between May 8, 1964 and July 1, 1967. Only one was set up in 1964, the one in Ontario. In 1966 three were set up. On April 6, 1966, the province of Nova Scotia set up the Nova Scotia housing commission. On April 7, 1966, the Prince Edward Island housing authority was established. In 1966 also the Newfoundland and Labrador housing corporation was set up.
Then, in 1967, four other provincial housing corporations came into being. I mention these figures to suggest, sir, that it is a little early to say that the provisions in the amendments of 1964 are not working. Perhaps it is not fair to single Ontario out because, undoubtedly, the housing pressures in Ontario are especially great; yet it can be noted that in Ontario at least 12,000 public housing units have been placed. The total for all Canada has been something like 16,000 units. In other words, approximately three quarters of all the public housing units to date are in the one province that set up its housing corporation in 1964.
The next province, in terms of numbers of public housing units, is Newfoundland and Labrador. This is followed by Manitoba. In Nova Scotia, up to the end of August, 1967, 321 public housing units had been placed.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
I say, sir, that the dates on which the corporations were set up and the number of units achieved are significant because they suggest that it is really too early to decide whether the amendments made in 1964 have been successful or have been failures. What is notable is that already in 1967 about $150 million has been provided for public housing projects throughout Canada by the C.M.H.C.

In addition, $52 million has been allocated for student housing; an additional $21 million has been provided for construction of housing for senior citizens; the sum of $55 million has gone for urban renewal; and 29 million for municipal sewage facilities. The total is over 300 million in this year alone toward the areas of greatest social need. Over $300 million has gone for those special kinds of needs in the housing field toward whose cost the taxpayer contributes openly.
This evening we heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) say it was to this field of public housing and to related areas of housing requirements that the government was proposing to give special priority.
The ceiling of 8J per cent applies in the field of what we call approved lender mortgages. What has been happening in this field is really very plain. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) when he made his announcement the other day, and the Minister of Finance tonight, have not attempted to conceal the truth. Those with money to lend have not found the rate of interest attainable sufficiently attractive. They have invested their money elsewhere. Consequently the number of houses built with conventional mortgages or with approved lender mortgages has not been as high as one might have hoped.
Confronted with this situation the government had two options. It could make it possible for approved lenders to lend money at rates more attractive to them. It could have raised the ceiling on the interest rate somewhat. Or, at the other extreme, the government could go out and borrow money itself to permit more and more C.M.H.C. loans at a rate below the open market interest rate. This presumably would have meant that the government itself would have had to pay more for the money it was borrowing. An alternative would have been to increase taxes. But no matter which way the government went about raising this additional money the basic result would have been the same. The taxpayer would be subsidizing the homebuilder to a higher extent.
Frankly, sir, that in itself does not jar me. All kinds of cross-subsidizations take place in our society; and cross-subsidization becomes more and more complex as our society becomes more and more complex. The point that must not be forgotten is that if this second option had been taken the taxpayer would be subsidizing a homebuilder to a higher extent.
I found that the hon. member for Saskatoon was confusing me a little on this point when he came out so strongly on the one
October 2, 1967	COMMONS
hand against subsidies and, on the other hand, insisted that unless the government reverses its policy the private homeowner will soon be driven out of existence.
An effort has been made to suggest that the high cost of housing is due to the expenditures of the government in other fields. This,
I think, shows that the opposition is underrating the genuine seriousness of the problem. As each topic comes up, whether it is the cost of food, the cost of education or the cost of defence, members of the opposition tend to resort to this narrow argument. They tend to insist that if the government would make savings in some other field it would not need to expend as much money on borrowing, and would not need to raise as much in the way of taxes. In other words, by tackling the various phases of government expenditure separately the opposition implies that the budget of the country is made up of watertight compartments. I do not think that is right at all.
We must think of the economy as something like a balloon. If you push it here it is going to bulge there. If you put more money into, let us say, old age pensions, it is going to have its effects on other parts of the economy. That is why the comments which the Minister of Finance made earlier this evening were so relevant, and I was so pleased to note that the members of the opposition were listening so attentively.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday, September 26, as recorded in Hansard at page 2484, I addressed this question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Mac-Eachen):
In view of increases that have taken place In the cost of living, and in view of the amendment respecting this matter which was written into the Old Age Security Act in 1965, has it been determined that there will be an increase in old age pensions this coming January and, if so, by what amount?
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
When I asked the question, Mr. Speaker thought it was not quite appropriate for orders of the day. Accordingly I posted it for one of these late show periods. In asking this question, I wish it to be clear that I am quite aware of the provision in our law under which the old age security pension, also the supplement that is attached to it in some cases, and the Canada Pension Plan are to be escalated. The provision is that each January there can be a percentage increase in these pensions if the consumer price index has gone up by a certain amount for the previous
October 2, 1967
2742	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion year. There is a formula in the statute which indicates how this is to be calculated and so on. The statute provides that a consumer price increase of less than one per cent is to be ignored and that a consumer price increase of more than two per cent does not result in an increase in the pension of more than that figure, namely two per cent.
The cost of living index, or the consumer price index as it is officially known, has been rising quite a bit lately. It follows, I have no doubt, that there will be a statutory increase in the old age security pension this coming January. The reason I asked the question was that I was anxious to know whether the necessary regulations had been passed and whether the necessary determination had been made so that an announcement could be made which would let our people know that the increase which is provided for is actually going to take place.
It was also my purpose in asking my question to get a clear statement as to what the amount of the increase will be. I realize that the legislation has in it a ceiling. It says that the increase cannot be more than two per cent in any one year. I should like, however, to express the hope that even after the government has made the announcement, which I trust will now be made tonight, it will face up to the fact that under the present circumstances an increase of only two per cent is hardly fair to our senior citizens
I do not wish to burden this house at this time of night with a great list of figures, but I have one or two which I should like to give. The consumer price index for October, 1963, stood at 133.6. The reason I give the index for that month in that year is because it was in October, 1963, that the old age security pension first became $75 a month. The consumer price index for August, 1967, which is the latest figure I have been able to get so far, stood at 150.9. In other words, from the date the old age security pension was set at $75 a month to the present time there has been an increase in the consumer price index of 17.3 percentage points. I do not wish to confuse anyone by seeming to imply that 17-3 percentage points is 17.3 per cent. So, let me make it clear that when you start out with 133.6 and go up 17.3 percentage points you have made an actual increase of 12.9 or almost 13 per cent.
In the face of this 13 per cent increase in the cost of living since the old age security pension was fixed at $75 a month I plead with the government not to be satisfied with


an increase in the old age security pension in January of only two per cent. I suggest that to use the argument that this is all the statute provides is not good enough. I am sure parliament would readily accede to an amendment to the statute to allow for an increase comparable to the increase in the cost of living itself. A 2 per cent increase in the $75 pension will provide an increase of only $1.50 per month. A 13 per cent increase, which would be comparable to the increase that has taken place in the consumer price index, would amount to $10.75 per month. I am aware of the fact that this increase will apply not only to the basic $75 pension but also to the $30 per month supplement in the case of those who meet the income test and are receiving it. In other words, if a person is receiving the $30 supplement he will get an increase of 60 cents as well as the $1.50, making a total increase of $2.10 per month. I am also aware of the fact that those drawing Canada Pension Plan benefits will get the same percentage increase. However, I plead with the government, in the light of the tremendous increases that have taken place in the consumer price index, to realize that it is not good enough to talk now about an increase of only 2 per cent or $1.50 per month in pensions. I hope the government will now make the appropriate announcement as to what is going to be done, and I hope it will also indicate that a way will be found to do better than merely increasing the pension by 2 per cent. Obviously, this is not enough.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Mac-Eachen) to advise the house whether or not the monthly payments made to nine provinces by the Canadian government under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act are up to date as of September, 1967, and whether the payments to the province of Quebec under the Interim Fiscal Arrangements Act are also up to date as of September, 1967. This question was preliminary to a supplementary question I intended to ask.
I do not have the slightest doubt but that the payments that should be made by the Canadian government to individual provinces on behalf of hospital services are being made in the proper amounts and on time. That is only proper and I am sure that the Minister of National Health and Welfare would see to it that this duty of his department was carried out religiously and accurately.
Over the week end I went to the city of Montreal to visit a married daughter who lives there, a married brother who lives in Beaurepaire, a cousin on the staff of the Montreal Protestant School Board and a niece who lives in Montreal. During that time I visited a large number of friends. During this visitation from Saturday to Sunday I was absolutely scandalized to learn that there are hospitals in the city of Montreal which have not received a single cent from the Quebec government department of health; in the case of three hospitals for over six months and in the case of one hospital for more than a year.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
The fact that the department of health of the provincial government of Quebec is not making the normal remittances to cover the operating expenses of these Quebec hospitals is putting the hospitals in dire straits financially. It is not incumbent on me to investigate all the hospitals and I do not have the time to do so. But in this case I had friends on the boards of governors of four of the large hospitals in Montreal and I confirmed the facts that were produced to me. These facts were attested also by members of the medical staffs.
