Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
Surely, if the Dominion of Canada is making payments to the Quebec department of health under the Interim Financial Arrangements Act, since Quebec opted out of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, the taxpayers of Canada are entitled to an explanation as to why the hospitals of the province of Quebec are in dire financial straits at the present time because they are not receiving any payments whatsoever from the provincial government of Quebec against their operating accounts.
I have made inquiries in the proper places and I know that no hospital in Canada outside the province of Quebec has any reason to complain about the speed with which their accounts are covered by the provincial departments of health. This includes the nine provinces outside of Quebec. Why is it that the province of Quebec, where they claim to be so much smarter than the officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare and its minister in Ottawa, where they claim that they can run their own hospital scheme much better than anybody else, is the only province in which hospitals complain that they have had no remittances from the department of health of the province to cover their operating expenses? I believe that the taxpayers of Canada are entitled to an explanation on this score.
We are a very heavily taxed country. The taxpayers of this country realize some of their taxes are being remitted to a provincial government which at no time makes any effort to explain the manner in which those funds are spent in the province, but stands up and makes the statement that the provincial government will establish the priorities under which expenditures shall be made. When this money is provided by the federal government in Ottawa, I think that the taxpayers of Canada are entitled to an explanation as to what is happening to the money the federal government takes from them and turns over to the provinces.
The other nine provinces do not hesitate to explain the manner of spending the federal funds that are entrusted to them under these shared-costs programs for hospital service. Why therefore, can we not get an explanation from the province of Quebec as to why the moneys sent to Quebec city from Ottawa are not used, apparently, for this purpose? I know for a fact that these moneys are remitted every month. They are remitted properly and on time.
Why cannot these federal funds reach the individual hospitals, even if the province of
2744	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Quebec decides it is not going to send the proper grants to those hospitals to cover their operating accounts? This policy of opting out of shared-cost programs is endorsed by some people who are not very familiar, I am certain, with human nature or cost accounting, because when a province opts out it then makes the claim that it does not have to explain its expenditures. It does not have to tell the government, in this case the dominion government, how it is spending the money which the government remits to it on the basis that it will be used for hospital purposes.
I know that no moneys are being advanced by the province to these four hospitals. One hospital in Montreal has not received a remittance from the Quebec government for over 12 months and the board of directors are at their wits end. A hospital in Montreal that has hundreds and hundreds of beds only last week had an order with the printers for letterheads, statements and order forms simply to replenish its supplies. The printer asked the hospital for cash on the barrel-head and also asked it to send a truck to pick up the supplies. Suppliers are simply refusing to forward any materials to these hospitals because of the delay in money being remitted by Quebec city.
Is this money being squandered on Expo? We are always hearing tremendous praise of the province of Quebec because of its great contribution which has made Expo such a success. If they have made such a success of Expo by withholding the proper funds from the hospitals which are entitled to the money and are using moneys that are sent to Quebec city by the federal government for hospital purposes, then this is a crying disgrace and I believe the federal government should give an explanation to the taxpayers of Canada as to why the hospitals in the province of Quebec are not receiving the money that the federal government remits to Quebec. Even if the federal government cannot speak for the province of Quebec, surely it can ask for an accounting of its remittances. There are many Canadians in the nine provinces outside of Quebec who take ill in Quebec and who, because of the portability of the hospital schemes in the ten provinces, are treated in Quebec hospitals. I believe that considering the fact that federal funds are being remitted to Quebec for hospital purposes and considering the number of Canadians from the other nine provinces who are treated in Quebec hospitals as a result of accidents or illness which they suffer when travelling through

DEBATES	October 2, 1967
that province, the federal government is entitled to an explanation as to what is happening to the federal tax moneys being remitted to Quebec for hospital purposes once every month, on time and in full. We know now that the hospitals in Quebec are not receiving grants regularly from the provincial government in Quebec city. I could name four hospitals in Montreal, three of them large, which have not received a cent in six months from the provincial department of health, while another large hospital has not received any remittance from the Quebec department of health in more than 12 months.
This cannot continue and I believe the Canadian government should ask for an accounting of what is happening to the federal hospital funds being remitted to Quebec city under that heading.

subsubtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES UNDER HOSPITAL LEGISLATION
speechtext:
All provinces, except Quebec, submit monthly claims for advances which are paid within a few days of receipt; Quebec being the only province to exercise its right under the Established Programs (Interim Arrangements) Act, submits estimates of cost which, after examination by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, (Mr. Mac-Eachen) form the basis for calculation by the Minister of Finance for tax equalization payments.
As of September 30, 1967, all advance claims received had been paid; three monthly claims had not yet been received at that date (Newfoundland, New Brunswick and Northwest Territories). My colleague, the Minister of Finance, (Mr. Sharp) informs me that the monthly equalization payments for Quebec are up to date.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
subsubtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MINT-INQUIRY AS TO PRODUCTION OF CENTENNIAL COINAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the last few months, starting in June, I have asked a series of questions on the apparent shortage of new centennial coinage throughout Canada. My reason for asking these questions was that one does not see this coinage in the tills, at the banks or anywhere in Canada, except for the odd coin. I think the idea of 1967 centennial coinage was an excellent one but I do not think that its distribution has been carried out very well. My question related primarily to the west because in the beginning there was some centennial coinage in eastern Canada but very little in western Canada despite inquiries by
October 2, 1967

banks, commercial institutions and ordinary people as well as coin collectors. It was impossible to get hold of these coins.
When I first made my inquiries the minister replied that regional distribution was not good. I brought it up several more times as I was interested more specifically in the total amount of centennial coinage turned out by the mint as against the total amount of old coinage.
The minister's answer to that question was that this year commercial shipments had been in excess of new centennial coinage by 42 per cent over regular coinage of 1966. If that is so, very little of it ever found its way into people's hands. I am referring to actual shipments. I have asked many people in banks and various stores across the country whether they had seen these new coins, and many of them had not even had a peek at a penny.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
There is no question in my mind that there has been a serious shortage. I do not care what the minister's figures are. I tried to follow up my question about the 42 per cent increase this year with a supplementary and to ask whether the centennial coinage was proportionate to the ordinary minted new coinage, but I received no answer. Perhaps I will get one tonight.
Then to cap it all, Mr. Speaker, today 1 asked the minister whether the mint had cut off the supply of coinage. I asked the same question in not just one or two but a number of banks, and I was told: "We have not seen any new coins for the last three or four months". This has been the answer I received in many branch banks, and one of the main branches in Ottawa even went further than that. They have not seen any despite the fact they have probably asked for them. I take it that the normal currency outlet for new coinage is the banking institutions.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, today I asked the minister whether production of this centennial coinage had been cut off at the mint, and his answer was no, but in fact the intention was to supply currency needs with 1967 coinage and not to carry the design forward into 1968.
The sort of question I am asked in correspondence and other media is: Where is this coinage? We have all heard lots of stories about large shipments going here, there and everywhere. If you apply for new coinage in
DEBATES	2745
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion sets, you are told you can get new coinage in sets from the mint. But this is only soft pedalling the question. I am talking about 1967 coinage for the normal use of the people of Canada.
I do not know whether there is any answer or whether the government intends to push the mint and to tell them to grind it out. Or perhaps they will just stick to the coin sets. But the fact of the matter is that very few of these new 1967 centennial coins have been issued and are in circulation in Canada.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
subsubtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MINT-INQUIRY AS TO PRODUCTION OF CENTENNIAL COINAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the question put by my hon. friend, we did make an inquiry of the mint and I am glad to reply that the mint has been manufacturing and will continue to manufacture coins bearing the centennial wild life designs until December 31, 1967. These coins will be distributed across the nation through the agencies of the Bank of Canada.
At the present time the mint has three full shifts employed in the coining and medal division. It is turning out approximately 12 million pieces per week of the various denominations. This is supposed to be sufficient to meet the requirements of the public.
They assure me that the procedure is to distribute the coins across the country in the normal manner. I do not know whether people such as collectors intervene in this process, but they do manufacture 12 million pieces per week and should be able to satisfy the demand. They cannot do more than this. As I say, they are working three shifts a day, so the mint is doing its best.
The matter raised by the hon. member tonight will be studied, and I hope that all those who want these new coins will be able to get them before the end of the year.
